utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution. Mr. Nicholls, I suppose today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, and Denise Gustin today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you all. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm David Cunningham with John Ackerman and as always assisted by Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have an hour and a half, Ms. Korner unless there are preliminaries, which I hope there aren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, and that's what I want to mention. Because when we looked at the questions Your Honours asked and the judgement, it's not a simple straightforward matter. We would prefer, and I believe Mr. Ackerman would concur with that, if we can put this in in writing which we'll do before Friday because it hasn't actually given a definitive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to discuss it myself obviously. But there are questions which are begged, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are a number of alternatives, and I believe we need to set them out for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is okay with you, Mr. Ackerman, as well, I would prefer it that way because it would give you an opportunity to go deeper into the matter. I intend to go deeper into the matter with my two colleagues and our staff as well because it is obvious. I know exactly what you have in mind. Thanks. Mr. Ackerman

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I agreed that would be an appropriate procedure, I didn't agree to this Friday. I can't make that. Can we say a week from Friday? I mean, they can file theirs on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not going to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they want to file theirs on Friday, I don't have any objection to that. But I just can't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have already fixed a schedule for ourselves how to spend the forthcoming days, so it doesn't really make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're quite happy with that as well. I simply said Friday in case Your Honours wanted it urgently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have plenty to discuss, Ms. Korner, as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then may I -- may I then return and just finish off yesterday's section with two documents. I was dealing generally with the media and propaganda, and I want to say a little more about it in specific relation to Mr. Brdjanin. But Your Honours, I would like to you to have a look, please, at two particular documents, one which Your Honours may remember is the -- generally called the document which is "The Curse of Lazar" issued by the Bosanska Krupa municipal board of the SDS. It's P2073. If we can put that up on the ELMO. And Your Honour will see down there, this was issued at the time of the referendum. It's an exhortation to Serbs to boycott it, and it ends with this remarkable, as it were, sentence: "The curse of Lazar will fall on each and every Serb despite everything he sees, knows, or hears, he chooses to cast his vote at the referendum." And it tells what you the curse of Lazar is. May no offspring male or female fill his heart with joy, may his hands -- something -- he was -- I can't read that, but anyhow Your Honours can see it. Your Honours, clearly the propaganda that was issued in -- by the form of leaflets and pronouncements from the SDS can go a lot further in many senses than what could actually be published in the, if I can call it, the proper media such the newspapers and the like, because this was an internal issuing. It wasn't likely to get the same kind of publicity if you like than if it was said to a television crew or to a newspaper. Your Honour, can I now ask you to look, please, at 2356. Your Honour, although it's undated, from the context it's possible to see that it's around the 6th of September, and it's -- it was issued by the Assembly of the association of Bosanska Krajina Municipalities, so it's before it's transformed into the ARK Assembly. And it's dealing with the mobilisation that happened September/October 1991. And you will see there that Mr. Brdjanin is quoted in this document issue. "Radoslav Brdjanin deputy president of the assembly gives this instruction." "We have no right, he says, to leave the Serbian people in Croatia to the mercy of the Ustasha warriors for our grandfathers would curse us and our grandchildren would be ashamed of us." We would suggest there's a similarity of language used by Mr. Brdjanin in this case to what -- much further in the Krupa document, because, Your Honour, the suggestion is that, as I say, Krupa is a completely -- a municipality that's off on its own. It has got no connections with any of the others. It's a renegade municipality. We say not. We say the same themes occur throughout. Your Honours, I'm going to turn now to for the next until I have -- until the next break to discuss Mr. Brdjanin in full, or concentrate on him, although obviously throughout what I've said over the last two days I have been linking the events and matters that I have been describing to him. Your Honours, he was, of course, we say one of the major propagandists of the Bosnian Serb leadership. There are very few other people who had the impact on the media and who said the things in the media that he did. Dr. Vukic, of course, was one of them, but you've heard evidence from a number of people, although in particular from the Witness BT-94, that although he could make terrible speeches, he wasn't regarded with anything like the same horror as Mr. Brdjanin, or anything like having the same authority notwithstanding the fact that he was the president of the municipal and regional SDS. Because he had this drinking problem. He was a man who could consume apparently 10 whiskeys a day without any difficulty whatsoever. So Your Honours, we say that Mr. Brdjanin, because of the positions he held, was much more the dangerous man and the person who incited, if nothing else, the crimes that were committed. But it's more than incitement. He had the authority to carry out the plan, not just incite it. Your Honours, if one just reminds ourself for a moment of his positions that he held during the period of the indictment, because a lot of people have said that was what gave him his authority. In November of 1990, he was elected to the Council of Municipalities in the multiethnic assembly of Bosnia. On the 19th of December 1990, he became the president of the executive council in Celinac. And that comes from a Defence exhibit, DB151. In April 1991, he became the first vice-president of the association of Bosnian Krajina municipalities. In September of 1991, vice-president of the Assembly of the ARK. April 1992, he was a member of the SOS Crisis Staff, and it looks like their chief spokesman. From the 5th of May to at least the 17th of July, he was the president of the crisis staff of the region. He was also appointed on the 13th of May to the ARK executive council as the secretary for the secretariat of traffic, communications, construction, et cetera. And on the 15th of September 1992, minister for construction in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, and then acting deputy prime minister. Now, there are very few people we have looked at in this case who held that number of positions. Now, Your Honour, I want to deal what is effectively the Defence's main point on his behalf, to counter all the other evidence that this case has shown that he was inciting and carrying out, a party to the carrying out of these offences. And that is what is described on a number of occasions as his saving of the 1.860 Muslims in Celinac. And so we think it's necessary to have a look at the background to that action, such as it was. Your Honour, the Defence in its final brief at page 139 stated that the Prosecution has at best proven that Brdjanin was an ambitious politician without any real authority or power behind the confines of the Celinac Municipality. And further claim that the exercise of his power and authority there are factors apart from anything else which are to be taken into mitigation -- as mitigation. Now, Your Honour, one needs to summarise what actually happened in Celinac between April and December of 1992 whilst the accused had real authority and power in that municipality. That's how it's described. Because as in every other municipality in the autonomous region that Your Honours have heard about, the Muslims and the very, very few Croats were driven from that municipality in fear of their lives. And like everywhere else, the direct perpetrators of crimes were neither prevented from committing those crimes, nor subsequently punished for the commission of those crimes. As Your Honours know, the Serbs were an overwhelming majority in Celinac. They formed approximately 88 to 90 per cent of the population there. Therefore, the non-Serb populations, the 2.000 or so Muslims, formed no threat whatsoever to the Serbs there. They held all the positions of authority in the government of Celinac. They, however, engaged, according to a report of the 5th Krajina Corps as it then was, on the 10th of March, and that's P363, that they engaged in arming the Serb population. The report also alleged that the Muslims in Celinac were being armed. And they noted in that report that the SDS had won the election and held all the power in Celinac. Now, about this time, Celinac addressed the -- Brdjanin addressed the Celinac Municipal Assembly, and this can be seen in P1999 at page 4. This was on the 31st of March 1992. And he gave his view very bluntly that with regard to the soldiers who have gone to the front, "we have tried to help many of them. No one can harm them or accuse them of being war criminals." In other words, whatever they may be doing at this stage in Croatia or wherever, they couldn't be war criminals. Now, it may well be, in fact, we would suggest it was, that the municipal authorities took those words to heart because the Celinac political leadership put pressure on the military court in order to obtain the release of the now notorious Sugic brothers who committed the murders in Celinac. Brdjanin, we say, on the basis of the documents - there's no evidence to contradict it - was on the 13th of May appointed to the Celinac municipal crisis staff. That's in P1993 and 1999, between pages 16 to 22. Your Honour, the witness, Mr. Talic, the Muslim Defence witness, confirmed that Muslims were disarmed in Celinac at the order of the police. It was put to him that the -- that there was an announcement on the radio saying that the Muslims had to surrender their weapons. It came from the -- it was suggested that was to the crisis staff on the 10th of May, so the same deadline. And he said, no, that wasn't correct. It was to the SUP in Celinac. And he was one of the people who had a weapon, a proper license. But nonetheless, he surrendered it to the police. That's at transcript page 24161. And Your Honour, it's confirmed by the SJB at a meeting of the Celinac Assembly that in Celinac, none of the non-Serbs have weapons. That was later on, on the 5th of August of 1992, and is at page 36 of P1999. Yes, sorry. I have been saying 199. It's all 1999. It's that long series of documents. Thank you. Your Honour, in June of 1992, in this overwhelming Serb Municipality, the attacks on Muslims' homes, businesses, and mosques began. This was documented contemporaneously in news reports and also verified by the witnesses that Your Honours have heard from at this trial. And the attacks followed the same pattern. The businesses and homes were blown up. Your Honour, can I remind Your Honour without having to put the exhibits up, P1991, Radio Banja Luka report of the 11th of June. And this was confirmed by the witness who gave evidence in closed session at pages T -- transcript pages 17072 to 3. On the 12th of June, the mosque was damaged and subsequently destroyed. And that's P1992, the item of the 12th of June. Both witnesses, that's the Defence witness and the Prosecution witness, confirmed that was right. And ultimately, the two mosques in Celinac were destroyed. Those attacks, those bombings that took place on Muslim residences terrified the Muslims and prompted them to leave. And that, too, was confirmed by Mr. Talic. At page 24164, it was put to him that he had said the Muslims had left Celinac because they were in fear. Is that correct? And he said: "Correct. Question: "What was this fear about? What was it based on?" "First, he said, let me tell you. There were intimidations going on. Fire. 24 houses are set on fire. Mosques were blown up." Now, the evidence was that Brdjanin attended a meeting between the SDS and Muslim leaders in July. This was after the killings that took place in Popovac -- I'm sorry, after the -- yes, the Sugic brother killings of the people returning from the meeting. And Your Honour, what the evidence is that Mr. Brdjanin said during that meeting at which Mr. Talic was not present was this: "Celinac was Serbian. Muslims and Croats would not live there, and the Serbs would find a way for them to move out." That is, Your Honours, at pages 17082. And to the people who were present at the meeting, it was abundantly clear what was meant by that. Your Honours, as I say, Mr. Talic didn't attend these meetings, and he was unable able to help the Court on that aspect of things. And in fact, he explained, Mr. Talic, that he didn't spend a lot of time in Celinac, he was either in Banja Luka or Orasje or on work obligation. Your Honours, that's at page 24172. Now, Your Honour, by the -- the effect was pretty dramatic because by the end of April of 1993, from the document P1981, there were only about 770 Muslims left in Celinac. Your Honour, it's also worth remembering that this is the municipality that produced what is possibly the most discriminatory document of any of the municipalities. And that was the document issued on the 23rd of July 1992 by the war presidency of which Brdjanin was a member, regulating the status of the non-Serb population in Celinac. It's P1998. And Your Honours will recall it prohibits movement, gatherings, and whatever. And one witness I think described it as a Nazi law effectively. And Your Honour, there's no question but that that document was disseminated. A number of witnesses even outside the municipality were aware of it, and it's the document that the Celinac Municipal Assembly when it re-met to verify the decisions taken by the crisis staff, refused to verify that. Your Honour, by the end of August 1992, the members of the Celinac Light Infantry Brigade, the Sugic brothers, and members of the CSB special unit or special detachment as it's called were engaged in these murderous attacks on the Muslims of Celinac. There were killings in the villages of Basici and Mehovci. Indeed, it was raised in the assembly. Your Honour, the Sugic brothers came under the command of Major Janko Trivic. And Your Honours, the major spoke at the municipal assembly. This is P1999, at page 42. And he was saying that he had seen the Sugic elders, and they have promised not to do it again. However, said Major Trivic, they continue to do it. And he said, and here we have the clear liaison and cooperation, coordination, whatever one likes to call it, between the political and the military side. He said, it is now up to you to decide what you will do next. With regard to this, the municipal assembly should establish crisis points and select two assemblymen who will spend three days studying the problem. Your Honour, if one recaps and summarises what the situation was by the time we come to the 1.860 Muslims in this municipality where the accused, it is conceded, accepted, had real power and authority, Serbs had been armed. Non-Serb population had been disarmed. Attacks had taken place on property owned by the Muslims. The mosques were destroyed. Brdjanin was saying that Celinac was a Serbian municipality and they would have to leave. They began to leave. That decision in July had been issued. And the killings had started. And Your Honour, that's the context in which the accused's alleged rescue of all the Muslims in Celinac has to be seen. Your Honour, when one comes to the events of the 18th of August, there is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps about what happened, and that is P2000, that it reports on the killings that took place in the Bastasi village and what had happened there. And as a result of those attacks, the Muslims of Celinac gathered in the centre of town. They couldn't return to their homes, and they couldn't leave because of the danger of attack. As the 1st Krajina Corps put it in its report of the 17th of August, because of some killings in the light infantry brigade, the Serbs were Celinac had decided to take its revenge on the Muslim population around Celinac. Your Honour, there was a witness, and can I just commend to you, who gave evidence about what happened at the school. That's transcript page 15478 to 15489. And we suggest that if Your Honours look at that testimony, Mr. Kovacevic who was the president of the municipal assembly and the former crisis staff president went to ask the 1st Krajina Corps what to do about the Muslims, that the security chief, Colonel Blagojevic was sent with others to deal with that problem. And we suggest that on that evidence, it was the 1st Krajina Corps who ordered Kuzmanovic not to harm the Muslims. And that's perhaps clear. It was a centre of attention clearly, Celinac. It's very close to Banja Luka. The idea that you should harm the 1860 Muslims who were gathered together in fear for their lives on the green that Your Honours may recall seeing between the municipal assembly and the hotel where the founding session of ZOBK was held. And Your Honour, the evidence also was to this effect: That Brdjanin was present at this meeting, as was Stojan Zupljanin. Your Honour, we suggest, therefore, that to say that Brdjanin was responsible for saving those Muslims is an overstatement. Mr. Talic, of course, gives Mr. Brdjanin full credit for that. It may well be that's because he isn't aware of the full facts and also because from his point of view, Mr. Brdjanin helped him save his daughter. She was in Kotor Varos. And that is a very interesting aspect of this case. Because it's suggested over and over again that Brdjanin had no authority outside Celinac and that if he went to visit the front line or wherever it was, he had to get a permit, whereas Mr. Radic didn't. One of the points that's made. But Your Honour, in fact, you may remember, Your Honours may remember, that Mr. Brdjanin, according to Mr. Talic, was able to provide Mr. Talic not only with a car - and Your Honours, this is at page 24186 of the transcript - a driver, but also a special permission permit "which enabled me to bring my daughter over to Celinac. I crossed a Serbian checkpoint in Kotor Varos, and they allowed me to go through." And at 24187, he explained how he went up to the municipality building and went to look for his daughter. And he -- there was a description of how he explained or the officer there had seen that he had been given permission by a Serb. And this officer said: "Well, we are fighting Muslims, and here it is we have a Muslim in the car. And then they understood that I was on friendly terms with Mr. Brdjanin, and I was allowed to go on on foot." Your Honour, it's clear from that alone that Mr. Brdjanin's authority extended well beyond the confines of Celinac. Your Honour, finally, if one reminds oneself very quickly of the Sugic brothers, they were finally, finally, detained and charged with the murders. And as with nearly every other Serb arrested for killings - we've deal with that in our final trial brief - they were released and returned to their units. Having been arrested at the end of 1992, as a result of a motion filed on the 26th of January, they were released, and the motion specifically cited the recommendation of the Celinac Municipal Assembly Executive Board for their release, together with the intervention of their commander and a petition signed by all the inhabitants of Mr. Brdjanin's own hometown, which was Popovac. So Your Honour, if one looks at all of that as a background to what happened, we suggest it is not the overwhelming mitigation that the Defence suggests that it is, nor does it suggest that that was the only place that he had power. Your Honours, we suggest that that was but an example of the power that he could exert. And if he could do it, then why didn't he do it in any other municipality? Why didn't he say "these Muslims should not be harmed" wherever it was, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, where his authority ran. Your Honour, one of the aspects I say, of course, of the cooperation between the military and the various crisis staffs, including the regional, what I failed to touch on yesterday was this: Apart from any other authority, cooperation, coordination which is shown, the municipal authorities, and in particular, the regional authority, because one of the major problems the municipality were having was supplies, and you recall the evidence, they were going up to discuss oil, was to cut off all supplies to the intervention squad that they knew was committing offences, to the military units, to the TO units, to say "we will not provide you with food, we will not provide you with the weaponry or the money or whatever." It may well be that it was a standard procedure with the old JNA that that was what the municipalities were expected to do. That may well be. But they had the ability, and in particular, Mr. Brdjanin, through the regional crisis staff, to say "your men are committing crimes. Until you stop them, we will not carry on supplying you." And who knows then what might have happened? Oh, yes, I'm sorry, I should give -- the exhibit number of the motion is P528, to release the Sugic brothers. Your Honour, in the remaining time, can I pick up the particular aspects of matters I've already gone through that reply to -- sorry, that apply to Mr. Brdjanin. Your Honour, his role in the early stages of the plan. At the -- in the Defence final brief, at page 110, they say: "Mr. Brdjanin never joined in a common design and was heavily criticised for his failure to do so." And later, at page 130, they say: "It is untenable to argue that in the light of this kind of criticism - that's from the Sansko-Usko group of municipalities - that the defendant was part of any joint criminal enterprise bent on achieving the strategic goals announced by Karadzic and Krajisnik." Your Honours, we've looked at some of the intercepts. And Your Honour if one just runs through some of the major ones, as early as the 17th or 18th of June 1991, there's a record of a telephone conversation between Mr. Brdjanin and Karadzic with Mr. Brdjanin complaining, even at that early stage, because a number of Muslims and Croats had not been removed from managerial positions in the media and companies. Not a single man has been replaced. And Mr. Karadzic expressed his support to Mr. Brdjanin and agreed that part of the SDS policy was the need to remove non-Serbs from managerial positions. Mr. Radic at one stage agreed that he was one of the architects of this policy. He said one of the smaller ones, but nonetheless one of the architects. And we say the evidence shows clearly that this persecution which started very early on and continued throughout was partly, at least, the brainchild of Radoslav Brdjanin. Your Honour, and I'm now not going to deal with every intercept or every speech made by Mr. Brdjanin in public. But on the 12th of July 1991, there was an SDS assembly, and Mr. Brdjanin attended it. And he set out his personal creed which we say is extremely applicable here and is if you like the epitome of the joint criminal enterprise or the chain of authority. He said: "I am a man who abides by two principles. I obey and respect those who are above me. All those who are under my command must obey me." And Your Honour, that is at -- it's Exhibit P2611, and I can't remember the page number. But it's in there. Your Honour, he put those principles into effect, we say the evidence shows, in the various positions of authority he held during the period of the indictment. Your Honour, on the 28th of July of 1991, a further intercept records a conversation between Brdjanin and Karadzic, again talking about the issue of the removal of non-Serb managers. And they also discussed the implementation of the SDS policy. Your Honour, there was a conversation between Karadzic and Stevandic on the 17th of August 1991. And it may well be that the reason that Mr. Stevandic notwithstanding his criminal activities was able to be on the various crisis staffs is because he was clearly a man who was close to Karadzic. And he said this: "Since we put Brdjanin into the picture, he is not letting Vojo - by that we take it he means Kupresanin - and Andjelko - that's Grahovac - do anything stupid. However, all of them have now turned against Brdjanin, not because of jealousy, but because they wanted to become involved in this part of the work." Your Honour, on the 18th of September 1991, again, in an intercept, there was -- between Karadzic and another gentleman named Komad who was the SDS Executive Board secretary, there was a discussion about getting Kupresanin, Brdjanin, Vukic and Radic together regarding mobilisation. And on the same day, the 18th of September, Mr. Brdjanin and Karadzic are recorded conferring over the phone on that issue, the mobilisation. And Brdjanin said: "I'm in charge of that - referring to the mobilisation - and the part that we're doing is going well." Throughout, the documents show that Brdjanin was linking himself very closely with mobilisation, the bringing in of troops and the like. There is evidence also from witnesses who were discussing these matters at that time, in particular BT-80. Yes. I'm sorry, I should give the exhibit numbers again. The intercept that is I discussed of Stevandic-Karadzic intercept P2355. And the next one where Brdjanin said "I'm in charge of that," P2382.8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. You did give the reference for the second intercept, that between Brdjanin and Karadzic where they discussed removal of non-Serbs the second time, at 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. 28th of July, the number there is 2382.4. Now, Your Honour, on the 23rd of September 1991, an intercept records Karadzic talking to Slobodan Milosevic. And he refers to Brdjanin as one of the persons who would implement the common plan in the Krajina because Milosevic was saying in general: "Banja Luka and Prijedor and those parts, some of those -- all of that should somehow constantly be kept in some kind of political readiness, under some kind of political influence." And Karadzic said this: "I don't know what's going on in the Krajina. I don't know who it is because I've told Brdjanin and Kupresanin. They're going there today to give them a speech. I think the people over there are happy to go." And then he said, there was further discussion about consolidation and so on and so forth. Then, Your Honour, on the 16th of October 1991 -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. The number for that is 2383.6. On the 16th of October, Brdjanin and Karadzic were deliberating about the Krajina and agreeing together that they should stop a movement to unite the Croatian and Bosnian Krajinas. According to the conversation, that was being spearheaded by Kupresanin and Grahovac. Certainly, Mr. Grahovac, we know from what was being done and said, was very keen on this idea. Your Honour, the telex, which I don't propose to go into detail about again, that was sent after the meeting in Banja Luka of the municipality presidents, which is referred to and indeed an assembly, to the presidents of the municipal assemblies. That's P22. Your Honour, the instructions bear some similarity to those in variant A and B about what is to be done. It could be said that this was a foreshadowing. It appears that the implementation or non-implementation was then discussed at an assembly meeting on the 6th of November. And one of the reasons given for that non-implementation was that in certain municipalities, the variant B municipalities, they couldn't be implemented. Because there the Serbs didn't have the authority. And that's P23, Your Honours. And Your Honour, finally, there are a number of different intercepts, including the one on the 18th of November which Mr. Radic listened to in the course of his evidence and identified the various voices, where again Mr. Brdjanin has rushed into print talking about the dismissal of non-Serbs. And Mr. Karadzic is telling him that "we were trying to treat it as a joke. I was trying to get you off the hook because you can't say that in public." They were trying at that stage still to keep the ideas covert ones. Your Honours, there are assembly meetings where he spoke, further meetings with Karadzic, Plavsic, and other leaders about which the Chamber has heard. And on the 7th of January 1992, there is a discussion between Karadzic and somebody called Miroslav. They're discussing candidates for leadership positions in the ARK, and Miroslav says "the principle ones are Dr. Jaksic and Brdjanin." And Karadzic said: "Find a political personality who will be able to take power." Miroslav: "Then it would have to be Brdjanin, I think." Your Honours, this is P2358, Exhibit 2358. Now, Your Honour, much is made in the Defence pre-trial brief of the outspoken criticism that took place of Brdjanin in early 1992, in particular at the end of February, the 28th of February at the meeting of the deputies' club. And the complaints, if I'm summarising, seem to be directed at the fact that the proposals that were made in the ARK Assembly for a separate Krajina state, the Republic of Krajina, were a product of Brdjanin's lust for power. But the concerns expressed reveal not only his importance, we suggest, but also how his extremist views which he was prepared to enunciate in public were being used by the SDS, the top leadership thereof, to achieve their goals. And the next day, many of that top leadership turned up to the 29th of February assembly in Banja Luka in order to make sure that this proposal for a Republic of Krajina, they were linking through the Krajinas, was once and for all squashed, and it was. And Your Honour, Dr. Donia, when he gave evidence, when he looked at all the documents, and this is at page 1150, said: "Yes, there clearly was a rift at some stage by the end of February. That was healed." Your Honour, the reality of the situation is as numerous witnesses have stated, the SDS exercised a rigid hierarchical control. And Brdjanin was able to assume the highest position in the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and remain there until such time effectively as the crisis staff was abolished and then he became a minister in the government. Your Honour, we suggest, therefore, that on the evidence, the assertion that he was not a party to any common plan which, as we say, the Defence appear to accept did exist, it cannot be maintained in the light of that evidence. In respect of the authority that he had, he did put that plan into effect in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And to the Muslim and Croat people in the ARK, there was no doubt that he held and exercised power and influence, and even some of the Serb witnesses called by the Defence, whilst attempting to minimise the effect of his role, and we suggest that is because they themselves were concerned in participation of these events, conceded that he did have real authority. I've already dealt with Mr. Radic saying he was a man of authority, not because particularly he was the president of the crisis staff, but because of all the other positions he held. BT-94 -- well, first of all, I should deal -- yeah, BT-94 who made assertions both in his diary and when he came to court, and some of the assertions that he made originally, Your Honours asked him to expand upon when he came -- returned to court. But he nonetheless stuck to this. He said: "In the context of the autonomous region, he was a big player, quite a big player. As for the Republika Srpska, I think even there, he was near the top, near the very top." And Your Honours, that was at page T18 -- transcript page 18169. "And after Brdjanin - he said - and the other three horsemen took over power, life became unbearable. Chaos set in. And Banja Luka turned into the biggest concentration camp in the world." Your Honour, interesting enough at the very early stages of this case when it was said, I think, originally by Mr. Krzic, there was a lot of cross-examination about why they were saying that and whether they got together, but a number of different witnesses used that very expression. Krzic said, if you live in a very practical concentration camp, you have to find ways to protect your life. Witness -- that was at page 1576. Witness BT-17, can I invite Your Honours to see what he said at T2835, because he testified in closed session, and then in fact Mr. Radic, although it was a different context, we accept, said Banja Luka was sealed off, cut off from the world at this period, 1992, that we are constantly discussing." Your Honour, when matters were happening like the arrival of the SOS or other important decisions were being taken, in particular on the 5th of April, it was Brdjanin and Mr. Vukic, but not Mr. Radic, the president of the SOS crisis staff, who went on to Banja Luka Radio to explain the implementation of the demands. It was Mr. Brdjanin who -- I'm sorry, that's Exhibit 2326. It's the diary. And P138. Your Honour, the 21st of April, and at other occasions, Mr. Brdjanin, when being interviewed, specifically named individuals who needed to be dismissed. And he issued the following threat: "If individual people in the Banja Luka companies who have been asked to withdraw do not do so in a period of three days, then members of the SOS will come on to the scene." On the 4th of May, and I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's P154. On the 4th of May, he said, again in an interview with Glas, when he was a member of the crisis staff and the commission for ethnic leveling of staff, "that managers who had voted for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina should leave their positions in the shortest possible time. Otherwise, they will be withdrawn by force and by members of the Serbian Defence Forces at that..." And that's P169. Now, Your Honour, that authority that he was using to issue those threats continued throughout his tenure as the president of the crisis staff of the autonomous region. Your Honour, I've already dealt briefly with the fact of his signatures. Those signatures not only went out under his signature block -- I'm sorry, those documents not only went out under his signature block, but in order to give them the added force, when Mr. Blagojevic was putting them into the Gazette, he added by each of the end of the documents that the original carried the signature of Mr. Brdjanin by putting in the words "SR," because that was important. It didn't matter, in effect, who did sign it, but what was important was that to the public and to the people to whom these decisions and orders were going were firmly of the impression that this carried the authority of the president of the crisis staff. Your Honour, on the signatures, as I say, the evidence has been from Mr. Blagojevic that he signed only -- actually signed only two or three. He said that other people were forging his signature. The real question was why was it necessary to forge his signature when the evidence was that if he wasn't there, and anyone could sign on his behalf, or certainly the vice-president? If there was whole scale forgery going on, and his secretary said not one single decision bore his signature, not even the one that was in the newspaper, the 22nd of June, the two that that was added in the Defence final brief the Defence conceded, and the ones they put in themselves. But the real question is: If there was whole scale forgery going on, who was doing it in and why? How is it that Mr. Brdjanin missed all of this? How does it square with Mr. Blagojevic's evidence that he was taking these decisions to Mr. Brdjanin for signature at the end of the day? No minutes, but decisions for signature. These decisions and conclusions did have a binding force, we say, equivalent to an order. And as Mr. Blagojevic put it when he was asked why the decisions had to be published in the Gazette: "It is a well known fact to make the general public aware of the decisions that were taken and how they were to be applied." And that can be seen at transcript page 21894. Now, on the 5th of May when Mr. Brdjanin appeared on Banja Luka Radio to talk about mobilisation, he was described by BT-94 as the mastermind behind all this madness. And when he came back, he was asked to explain it. He said: "It could hardly be put that way that Radoslav Brdjanin was the mastermind, that he conceived all of this. He was one of the creators of the self-defeating policy. This had to do with mobilisation," he said, "as far as I could see. He stood behind this self-defeating policy. He was a prominent proponent of this policy. Now what made me say this? Everything he said showed that this was a man who did not hesitate to use big words, and big words lead to big consequences. He labelled other ethnic groups and glorified his own. All of that was sufficient reason for me to view him the way that I did and to assess him the way that I did." Your Honour, that can be seen at page 24778. Now, Your Honour, the expression "puppet" was used by either Mr. Vidic or Mr. Dejanovic. I can't remember which of the two now. We say that the evidence that what Mr. Brdjanin did at these meetings, of all of the decisions, show that he was no puppet, but the driving force behind the major decisions that were being made. And those decisions were being implemented in the municipalities. Milorad Sajic's testimony at 23 -- at page 23703 shows that he was the constant factor in the crisis staff. He decided when it was necessary to hold a meeting. He summoned members to the meetings being sometimes at short notice. He was in charge of all the meetings, and the meetings could not start without him being present. And that's at -- I think I've given the reference already. Now, the Defence in their final brief between pages 156 and 165 dealt with the evidence of the internationals. Not with any of their descriptions of the events in Bosnia of what was happening, of what nearly all of them described as ethnic cleansing and more, but to underline the fact that none of them had any meetings with Mr. Brdjanin. And if they met anyone in Banja Luka, it was Mr. Radic. And they assert that that shows that he had no authority. Your Honours, we submit that all of that shows, all that shows is that he wasn't put forward as the person to meet. It is perhaps not surprising. The face that he showed to his own people, the face that could be seen in Banja Luka by the Muslims and the Croats and by the Serbs themselves was not one that they, the Serbs, were anxious for the international community to see. Moreover, of course, Predrag Radic was the municipal president or mayor as he was known to those who couldn't distinguish between the two. And he had been there since the elections of 1990. And undoubtedly, Your Honours may think from the evidence, whatever his true aspects were, he was the more user-friendly of the two men. That is what many of the victims themselves said. And the more user-friendly as far as the leadership was concerned. Your Honour, the documents and the testimony of those who were in Banja Luka, of those who were living in the municipalities, not just passing through, show the reality. Your Honour, in early August of 1992, when foreign journalists were arriving to inspect the camps, Mr. Brdjanin, together with Mr. Ostojic, appeared on Banja Luka Television. And Your Honour, he was moved to explain - I was going to show this video, but I think I'm running out of time - to say this: "We were surprised when the Muslim and Croatian people rose to fight in certain parts of Krajina. We were surprised for two reasons: Primarily we're good neighbours; and secondly, they don't stand a chance in the world. And those who are honest amongst those people must understand that at least here, on this territory, they don't stand a chance in this fight." Your Honour, that is the video P7 -- sorry, P2727. Your Honour, after the winding up of the crisis staff, Mr. Brdjanin was still a power to be reckoned with. On the 18th of August, he's attending the meeting with -- it's a political-police-military meeting in General Talic's office, which includes amongst others General Talic, Stojan Zupljanin, and the Air Force General Ninkovic. And can I make it absolutely clear that what was discussed there as we said in our response, we put in error camps, but the closure of the Omarska camp was being discussed there. And there were other meetings, and he was still making public statements. The public statements that he was making throughout were propaganda designed to terrify the Muslims and Serbs into leaving, designed to create the climate whereby these offences could be committed. I'm sorry, the Muslims and Croats. I see it has come out on the transcript as Muslims and Serbs. The Serbs who testified on his behalf themselves recognised the appalling nature of his public statements. Mr. Dejanovic said, "he has talked quite hard, also as Mr. Vukic. They talked very hard. Mr. Brdjanin especially during election campaigns, he was capable of saying anything at those public rallies, and he was able, including other SDS members, virtually competing in who would use more abusive language." That was Mr. Cvijic. And he added, as did some of the other witnesses, that this wasn't the real Mr. Brdjanin. He had two faces. One was for the public. And it was really inconceivable how this person could have said these things, and he had another face when he was at work. And Mr. Radic said something similar. Mr. Cvijic said that at page 21421 and Mr. Radic at 22006. Your Honour, the importance of this propaganda was really highlighted by one of the witnesses, and that's BT-19. Can I invite Your Honours to look at the transcript page 20654.

utterances.text: And one of the other witnesses, again, Your Honour can I refer to -- this was in closed session as well. Brdjanin, we say, and I don't think that there is, Your Honours, so much evidence about this that I think I'm simply going to invite Your Honours to go back to brief on this because we have listed quite a lot of the various things that were said. But I perhaps should add this in relation to the targeting part of Mr. Brdjanin's speeches: Particularly, when he was advocating the dismissals of the non-Serbs in positions of responsibility, he actually mentioned people by name. Mr. Osmancevic, the head of Metal, one of most successful business in Banja Luka, Mr. Fazlagic, who ran the travel agency. And one of the witnesses said -- I'm afraid it was in closed session as well. Can I ask Your Honour to look at Witness BT-17, please, at 2866, what he said was the result of this targeting by Mr. Brdjanin in the media. Your Honour, at the end of August, Mr. Brdjanin appeared on television to state, according to BT-94, the media watchdog as he's described by the Defence, which is perhaps not an inappropriate way of describing him, to say this: "Those who are not loyal are free to go. And the few loyal Croats and Muslims can stay. As Seselj said about the 7.000 Albanians in Kosovo, they will be treated like gold, and this is exactly how we are going to treat our 1.200 to 1.500 Muslims and Croats. If Hitler, Stalin, and Churchill could have working camps, then so can we. Come on, we are at war after all." Your Honour, those statements had a direct and positive impact on the non-Serb population, the Muslims and the Croats. The percentages that he gave of those that -- who would be allowed to remain, the figures, 1.200 to 1.500, the 2 to 3 per cent, those go, we submit, specifically to a genocidal intent he was expressing. Mr. Fazlagic at page 4273 talked about that speech. He said: "5 to 6 per cent, which meant that 95 per cent would have to leave their native land. I had to leave my town, a town that I had given everything to. And I'm wondering why I left. What did I actually do?" And another witness said: "In all the" -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's 4273 of the transcript. Another witness said: "In all the programmes, and especially on television, he, Brdjanin, publicly frightened people. And after that, people would leave Banja Luka and ethnic cleansing took place. I can say with certainty for Mr. Brdjanin that he was the alpha and omega of those programmes." Your Honours, that's at page 3264. Your Honour, I think it's only right that instead of just reading through what he said, Your Honours should be reminded of just two of the occasions that Mr. Brdjanin was on television. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That will do. Thank you very much. Now, Your Honours, the Defence make the point, and it's a valid point to this extent, that this was a rally that took place in 1993. But it shows in 1993 an intention which was almost unnecessary by then because certainly in most of the areas, the Muslims and Croats of the Krajina, the Muslims and Croats were gone. But it's not that so important. It's the way he describes them. "Non-Christian scum." Your Honour, this is a man who allegedly according to his secretaries, to Mr. Talic, really liked Muslims. Didn't have any animosity against them at all. Then why is he using those terms to describe the Muslim population? Your Honour, I've dealt now with the -- a sort of very quick overview of his speeches and the effect that they had. In the Defence final brief at page 207 -- it's the final brief, they say: "One must still question the extent to which the public had access to the defendant's purported statements." And they talk about the newspaper shortage and the electricity cuts. But Your Honour, the fact is everybody has said that they did have access, they did hear what he said. And even if they didn't hear it personally, because it was so terrifying, it was repeated to them. Your Honours, I've dealt with the intent, the specific intent that's shown by the percentages that he was raising, but in -- on the 10th of July, he gave what was called a selective press conference because Glas was complaining about it. It was to do really with the editorial policy of Glas. And he said: "The only way the Serbian people can be unified is through the promotion of the Serbian Movement for Liberation and the destruction of the Ustasha." Your Honour, that is Exhibit P2326. The famous Prijedor statement, 17th of July: Having visited Prijedor, including the Omarska camp, having undoubtedly seen the destruction that was being caused, he said, and it was quoted in Kozarski Vjesnik: "What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a job well done. And it is a pity that many in Banja Luka are not aware of it yet, just as they are not aware of what might happen in Banja Luka in the very near future." And that is Exhibit P284. The Defence themselves say Prijedor was the scene of some of the most horrendous crimes. Your Honour, it is said that's only Kozarski Vjesnik, and that can't be relied on. But there -- and he said, "there's no other evidence to support that." That's not right, in fact. Because (redacted) gave evidence before Your Honours. And this is at pages 12776 to 7, himself a journalist. And he was asked as to whether or not he had seen Mr. Brdjanin, and he said, yes, he had seen him after he had got out of Omarska on a programme on television. And he said the programme lasted for more than an hour, and was open to receive questions from viewers. And as far as I remember, the gist of the programme was that the accused here, Radoslav Brdjanin, commended the Prijedor Crisis Staff and the political leadership for having done a very good job in the territory of the Prijedor Municipality, that they cleansed the area very well in accordance to some plans. And I remember very well a sentence that he used, and it was a sentence often used by someone who shares his political views and who worked with him. And he mentioned the name of this other man. "Brdjanin repeated a sentence then, and the sentence is as follows: `All the non-Bosniaks who remained to live there', he said `all Turks or balijas who remain in the territory Serbian State will shake with fear. Their pants will shake with fear if they do not accept the laws of the Serbian state.'" Your Honour, these and the similar statements express a frank desire that crimes be committed and they were part of this campaign of propaganda in which the accused played the leading role. As I've said, and I repeat, the purpose to strike fear into the non-Serb population, and as importantly, to create the climate whereby if the fear didn't drive them out, then the crimes would be committed against them. Your Honour, finally, and this is the last thing that I want to say, the Defence in their final brief dwelt on this aspect of Mr. Brdjanin, in particular what was said about BT-94, suggesting that the defendant was merely the public face, and that the real power and authority lay elsewhere. And this, they say, of course, has been the defendant's claim from the start. They seem to realise that they don't want to mean it quite as the way it sounds, because footnote 443 on that page says that they don't mean that public face means equal spokesman, but that the public perception of Brdjanin and his actual power and authority are two different things. Now, that has not been the defendant's claim, that he was merely the public face from the start or any other time. On the evidence, however, both the public face -- I'm sorry, he was both the public face and indeed had authority. Others, like Vukic and Radic may also have had authority, but it was the "public face" who was responsible in the position that Mr. Brdjanin held for not only inciting the crimes, but for having the powers to issue those decisions that we've spoken -- that I've spoken about. The words "talked a good game" which is how the final brief talks about him at page 212, if I understand correctly that expression, in those circumstances "talking a good game" is criminal behaviour. Some witnesses have said that in their view, the reason for his actions was to advance his own political career, rather than an honest and genuine belief that the only way to create a Serbian state was to drive out and destroy the Muslims and Croats. And a number of witnesses have said that there was a real dichotomy between what he said and what he did in private with respect to non-Serbs and his public attitudes. And in page 212 of the Defence final brief, they say: "The defendant did not join in a common purpose with others. He was acting independently to further his own career." Of course, we say the evidence shows that he was, indeed, joining a common purpose. He was not acting independently. The words "to further his own career," very possibly. If so, that was his motive, and that cannot affect his intent. The intent, we say, that the evidence in this case clearly shows, the intent required for the commission of these offences. And we say, Your Honours, that it is all the more cynical and reprehensible that he did, or if he did all these things for no other reason, for no other motive than to further his own career, that is more reprehensible than the man who commits these offences out of genuine conviction and a desire to see the total extinction of the Muslims and non-Serbs. Your Honour, we say finally, if Your Honours consider all the evidence in this case, dispassionately and objectively, as we know that you will, then the only proper verdict -- verdicts, in this case, is one of guilty on all counts charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection goes to page 10 today, lines 21 through 23 where it was argued that the Defence had conceded and accepted that the defendant had real power and authority this Celinac. That is not our position. We do not concede that. We at best concede that he was a man of some influence in Celinac, but not sufficient to rise to the level of 7(3) responsibility or 7(1) responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Who's going first? Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it please the Court. As Witness B-20 recounted early in this trial, the problem faced by everyone trying to deal with the situation in the Krajina in 1991, in 1992, was the mere fact that people held offices or had titles, did not necessarily describe their authority, and it was often that people without titles were the people that were actually wielding the authority. Radoslav Brdjanin may have had titles, Your Honours, but he had no power, no authority, no subordinates, and he should be acquitted on all counts. If we were to distill the Prosecution's case to its essence, it comes down to their argument, and we see this, for example, in paragraph 183 of their brief that Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. Brdjanin was the most powerful civilian in the region, they allege, and served as an essential link between the republic leadership and the region. The second part in essence is that as head of the ARK Crisis Staff, the defendant had a great deal of authority over the municipal bodies, the police, and the military structures. As we've argued in our final brief and as we'll argue here today, we believe that these claims are not supported by the evidence, and Mr. Brdjanin is entitled to an acquittal on all counts. If we go back to early mid-1991 in Celinac, what we would find from the evidence is that Mr. Brdjanin is a man who enjoys some influence in that municipality. As I stated earlier, it's not the sort of influence or power that translates into 7(1), 7(3) liability as described in paragraph 263 of the Delalic appeals judgement. But if we look at the evidence in 1991, we'll see that there is a relationship between him and Radovan Karadzic. And while at first glance, it might appear to be a relationship that's based on mutual respect, it really isn't. Because we know by looking at all the evidence in this case, by the end of February, well before the formation of the ARK Crisis Staff, and I'm talking about February 1992, his relationship, Mr. Brdjanin's relationship with Mr. Karadzic, had deteriorated to the extent that they were both openly critical and contemptuous of each other. We know from the evidence that there was really no place for a regional body in Bosnia's political culture, in a political culture that was headed up by a strong central leader such as Dr. Karadzic and, and this is just as important, included strong, independent municipal leaders that were not about to give up the power that had been theirs for years.
