utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll put it on 33, Judge, rather 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. You're still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I invite both the Court's comments and the interpreters' comments if I'm going a little too rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Keeping that in mind, I would slowly like to discuss several areas that will show that the defendant and the ARK and the ARK Crisis Staff lacked political legitimacy. Political credibility. And the absence of his own political legitimacy. Political credibility in the absence of his own political legitimacy and credibility affected the way he was viewed by Sarajevo, then Pale, as well as by the municipalities. I'd like to discuss the evidence which I think shows that Karadzic quite candidly considered Mr. Brdjanin to be an incompetent, someone who constantly belittled him in public, and that this embarrassment, this humiliation, this criticism of Mr. Brdjanin affected Brdjanin's political legitimacy and the way that he was viewed. And I would also like in the course of my comments today to talk about some structural factors, what I will call for want of a better word, the institutional resistance to Mr. Brdjanin ever having any power. That institutional resistance comes in the form of two things: Number one, Dr. Karadzic, and what I'll call the upper echelons of the SDS. We'll see from the evidence that I talk about today that Dr. Karadzic was radically opposed to regional bodies. I'll also talk about the forces in the municipalities, the fact that despite what Ms. Korner may say, I believe the evidence has clearly shown that Mr. Brdjanin was not accepted in the municipalities. Yesterday, Ms. Korner said all municipal leaders had been big fish in small ponds. The municipalities were given a great deal of autonomy under the old Bosnian system, and no doubt they were most reluctant to surrender the autonomy. Ms. Korner makes the argument that ultimately they did. I submit the evidence supports the contrary position, that they never did. A good place to start, Your Honour, in tracing, if you will, Mr. Brdjanin's lack of political legitimacy and his falling out with Mr. Karadzic is the wire intercepts. Prosecution argues that these intercepts show that the defendant was a man of power and authority in the Krajina. But if we look at the intercepts as a whole, the very few that we have, we'll see fissures, breaks, in the relationship between Karadzic and Brdjanin, that by the end of October of 1991, I submit, that there was really no real respect between the two men. And by the end of February 1992, there was a wide, open schism, a wide, open break between the two, and that Mr. Brdjanin was openly contemptuous not only of Mr. Karadzic, but of the Pale power structure. And what despite what Mr. Karadzic may have alluded to in one of these intercepts, Mr. Brdjanin was devoid of any real authority and real power. When we talk about the Prosecutor's position and again trying to break their position with respect to these intercepts down to its most basic level, I think you can see their position contained in three paragraphs. Paragraph 192 of their brief says: "A review of the telephone intercepts shows that Brdjanin was committed to the planning -- to planning the SDS strategy." In paragraph 546, they allege, argue: "Intercepted phone calls show that the accused cooperated closely with Dr. Karadzic and the SDS leadership, and in Karadzic's words, the defendant `had all the power in the Krajina'." The Prosecution also makes much about Exhibit 2611. And this contains what they call Mr. Brdjanin's personal creed. This is a statement attributed to him 12 July 1991 in which he is quoted as saying: "I am a man who abides by two principles. I obey and respect those who are above me. And all those who are under my command must obey me." If this Chamber were to look closely at the body of the intercepts and the events that go into February of 1992, this personal creed that they place so much weight in about Mr. Brdjanin literally quite goes out the window. The first part of the creed we'll see from these transcripts is that, and the events that go into February, is that Mr. Brdjanin did not follow the orders and directives of those above him. And as we'll see when we look particularly at this one exhibit, one intercept, nor did he obey and respect those that were above him. The second part of that creed has to deal with his subordinates. The fact of the matter is when we look at the evidence as a whole, Mr. Brdjanin did not have any subordinates. Before I talk about these conversations that were intercepted conversations, I want to bring up a couple of points before I go into the actual body of the intercepts. During the course of their arguments and their presentations, the Prosecutor has argued that the defendant was given great autonomy and independence. And I submit to the Court that they cite this to you, they argue this to you to help on their part to try to explain the lack of any real meaningful, written, or telephonic communication between the ARK and Sarajevo, then Pale. The inference they're trying to get the Court to draw is the following: Because there was no communication between ARK and Pale, it must be due to the fact that the defendant was accorded great autonomy and independence. In reality, we believe the reasonable deduction from the evidence is that Karadzic had no place for the ARK, and after doing what he could through the upper echelons of the SDS, and through his ties to the municipality, to ensure that the ARK was impotent, largely ignored it. The second point that I'd ask the Court to consider when you consider the body of the intercepts is this: The range of the intercepted conversations before this Court, between Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Karadzic, goes from 17 June 1991 to 18 November 1991. Must ask, I believe, why are there no conversations between Brdjanin and Karadzic after the last one on 18 November? Why is it, the evidence has shown that 80.000 conversations were garnered by the wiretappers, if you will, in Sarajevo, why of those 80.000 conversations, why only these 13? If there was this close chain of command, if there was this Karadzic-Brdjanin working hand in hand, where are the records of any additional telephone communications between the two? And while an argument might be made, might be made, that the combat operations or the war might explain the absence of telephonic communications, why aren't there any written communications? If this is, as alleged by the Prosecution, an intermediate level of government, why aren't there not documents going up from Banja Luka to Pale or down from Pale to Banja Luka? I'd like to now start by looking at the wire intercepts and the events in the summer and fall of 1991. July 1991 is the date that we see a conversation, 2 July 1991, reflected in Exhibit P2382.2. This is a conversation between Brdjanin and Karadzic. And in this -- I don't think it's important to put it up on the ELMO, but I think if we read this, one of the things that you'll start to see is the derision, the condescension in Karadzic's voice when he is dealing, and in his words more importantly, when he is dealing with Brdjanin. Because when we look at this, there is a discussion in this intercept about a Serb army. And Karadzic literally has to lecture Mr. Brdjanin about what I call the fallacy of a Serb army. July is also important, Your Honours, because in July, Karadzic makes some statements about how he feels about regional bodies. And I'll come to that shortly. He's talking about, granted, regional bodies of the SDS, regional boards of the SDS. But I think from Karadzic's statements about regional bodies, we see his true attitude towards the ARK. We know that from the evidence, there is a dispute between Pale and Banja Luka about whether or not there should be an independent Krajina. We know from the evidence that the -- the people in Banja Luka had expressed displeasure at the republican government for not paying attention to them, and we know from the evidence that was presented that the people in Pale felt under Karadzic that it was repeating himself, that Karadzic was ignoring the people in Pale. And we see one of the manifestations of this dispute, this conflict between Brdjanin and Karadzic, on 13 July 1991. Reflected in Exhibit P13, which is the stenogramme or the notes of an SDS meeting on 13 July 1991, we see Dr. Karadzic making statements referring to people, and I'm quoting, as"power grabbers." He is condemning people with "power grabbing impulses" and "the little Napoleans who are trying to do things to harm the Serbian people." Those quotes that I gave, Your Honours, come from pages 25 and 28 of Exhibit P13. Although he doesn't mention Mr. Brdjanin by name, when one reads Mr. Karadzic's statements later on, it is obvious that he is referring to those people in Banja Luka that are pressing for an independent autonomous Krajina, and he is opposing that. Also in July, we see that there is another conversation that is intercepted. That is Exhibit 2382.4, a 28 July conversation, and in this conversation, again, by reading it, you can sense the condescension, the derision that Mr. Karadzic has for Mr. Brdjanin. There is a conversation in here about a referendum. And if you read that exhibit closely, you'll see that Dr. Karadzic is getting exasperated with Mr. Brdjanin. He says to Mr. Brdjanin, he has to put him in his place by saying, and I'm quoting Mr. Karadzic's words: "So please trust us in what we are doing, for God's sakes." That's at page 4. Now, is this a full-blown agreement between these two gentlemen? Of course not. What I'm suggesting is in July, we start to see a feud, a dispute, a conflict that's starting to simmer. And we see this going into October as well. Exhibit 2382.11 is an intercepted conversation between Karadzic and Brdjanin, 18 October 1991. This is referenced in paragraph 204 of the Prosecution brief. And here's what their brief says: "Karadzic is instructing Brdjanin by telephone on issues related to the implementation of the SDS strategy in the Krajina. Brdjanin responds positively to all instructions from Radovan Karadzic, in a way indicative of a common purpose." I ask the Court: Do the following responses made by Mr. Brdjanin in the body of this conversation support a claim that he is responding positively? During the course of this conversation, on page 1, page 2, Brdjanin says: "I don't want to get involved." Secondly, he is making the complaint that we hear so often through this trial, that "no one in Sarajevo was supporting them." No one was asking them to behave responsibly. And again, talking about the condescension, the attitude that Mr. Karadzic has to Mr. Brdjanin, he talks about - referring to Brdjanin - about childish games and talks about "slapping them and you," referring to Brdjanin. I suggest to the Court we're starting to see the fact that irrespective of what Mr. Karadzic may have said to Milosevic, there are problems between the two, and I think we can honestly say from the evidence that Mr. Karadzic is thinking that Mr. Brdjanin, with all due respect, is a foolish child. 31 October is another conversation, and I'd like to see Exhibit 2357, please. This is a -- if I could hand this to the usher, this is an exhibit that was talked about yesterday. And you get a clear picture of this growing rift between the two, and to put this in the context, this exhibit is the one that was discussed yesterday where Brdjanin calls up Dr. Karadzic talking about their having a dancing programme at the JNA hall while at the same time there have been 11 soldiers who have been in war and who have been killed. I believe it's on page 4 that we see Karadzic belittling him. And to be fair to the Prosecution, when you look at this brief in -- this brief, this intercept in its entirety, there are points that they argue that are very, very important. And in all fairness, I'll bring them out because Karadzic says "if you are capable of governing the Krajina, then do it properly, damn it." Civilian government is in your hands. That's what Karadzic says to him. He also says: "You have all the power. Why don't you exercise it? If Stojan is no good, dismiss him." But I want to point out some of the things that the Prosecutor didn't bring out in this conversation. Interestingly, the Prosecutor didn't point out in the very same conversation, Karadzic says: "You call me about every little thing, and that proves your incompetence. " There's even a reference in there where Karadzic says to him "what am I, your nanny?" He says to Brdjanin: "Don't give me proof of your incompetence. If you can't cope, put a group together that can." It's kind of interesting, although I find another point interesting in this, in that Karadzic tells Brdjanin that Radic should have declared a day of mourning. And that's on page 3. And I don't think it's important to look at that right now. But I want to bring, while we're talking about what Karadzic says and these attributing power and authority to Mr. Brdjanin, I want to remind the Court that something that Lord Ashdown said when he came before this Court and he told this Court at page 12415 of the transcript, and he's talking about Karadzic and his dealings with Karadzic. And this is what he said about Karadzic: "Karadzic was able to lie to you straight to your face in a way more convincing than any man I have met." And I submit to Your Honours that Lord Ashdown's experience, his dealings with Karadzic, give a really good insight into his personality and to take Karadzic's statements at this point as the gospel truth is unwarranted because of his personal character, but more importantly as the subsequent political events show. Thank you, Mr. Usher. The next conversation is 9 November, that I want to talk about, is 9 November 1991. And this is important because in this conversation, we see what Brdjanin, Mr. Brdjanin, thinks of Pale, what he thinks of Karadzic. And as we go through this, I'd like the Chamber to ask themselves these questions: Is Exhibit 2382.12 indicative of what the Prosecution claims is the evidence of the close cooperation between Karadzic and Brdjanin? Is this an indication of the personal creed where obedience and respect are essential? Can I have that exhibit, please. This is the conversation where Mr. Brdjanin calls up the SDS looking for Mr. Karadzic, but apparently Mr. Karadzic and his cohorts are at a party somewhere, so he's left talking, Mr. Brdjanin is, to the duty officer. That's not reflected on their screen right now. But on page 1, there's conversation, Brdjanin is talking about the blue helmets, obviously the UN in Sarajevo. But on the second page, we see some of the things that he said. Brdjanin says: "We renounce our loyalty to the army. We renounce our loyalty to the SDS, to everyone, everybody has tricked us. And feel free to say that if Karadzic or someone else stops by, Brdjanin telephoned, and he will say just let Brdjanin talk. But all of them who say that will deeply regret it. We do not trust anyone any more. We are going to organise ourselves on our own. Neither Karadzic nor anyone else should come to the Krajina any more. He lied to us. We were going for the creation of a state. We will call a plebiscite, and those pigs, one next to another, you know, are calling in the blue helmets while they are celebrating in the Holiday Inn" and then we see what other language he used. That is not an individual that is showing obedience, respect, for allegedly those who are above him. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm done with that. By this stage, the end of -- the first part of November, the stage is set for full-fledged conflict between Pale and Sarajevo and Banja Luka, because I think the evidence clearly shows what Brdjanin thinks of them. He is, to put it mildly, distressed because they are ignoring the Krajina. And we know from Karadzic's statements from the conversation that I talked about earlier, Karadzic quite candidly thinks Brdjanin is an incompetent. This simmering dispute that I talk about in the fall of 1991 becomes a full-fledged dispute, fully boiling, by the end of February. The events in February, I submit to the Court, are important because they affect the political legitimacy, the political credibility of Brdjanin, and the ARK Crisis Staff. This --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. And please, interrupt me at any time. This conflict is one of the many factors that we submit ensures that neither the defendant nor the ARK, nor the ARK Crisis Staff have any real power, real legitimacy. I think at this stage, I'd like to take a step back and devote just a few minutes to talk about the political culture in the former Yugoslavia because that political culture, particularly in Bosnia, affects the way that the upper echelons, the Karadzic, and the municipalities view the ARK, the new comer, the novelty on the scene. In his testimony, Dr. Shoup talked about the long history of central government, and he used the phrase that central government called the tune in the former Yugoslavia. I suggest to the Court that that sort of ingrained, political culture doesn't change overnight, and that the events in this case show that to be actually the case. The ARK was the new kid on the block. It was a novelty. And because of forces in the upper echelons and in the municipalities, we suggest that it was doomed to failure before it even started. Why was it doomed to failure? Well, the reasons come from many different ways. We know that there was no way, based on Dr. Donia and I think Patrick Treanor's testimony, they both talked about the notion of sociopolitical communities and their unique status in the former Yugoslavia. But neither of them said that the regional bodies were a sociopolitical community. So that tells us it doesn't fit into the political culture. But more importantly, the president of the party was not about to give up any of his powers, and we know it's a strong, centralised party. We know from looking at the evidence, and this is where I'm going to talk about what Karadzic said about the regional bodies. In July of 1991, I alluded to this earlier, at P13, which again are the notes from the SDS session of 12 July 1991, Karadzic is quoted at page 27 of paragraph -- excuse me, of Exhibit P13 about how he feels about, granted, regional boards of the SDS. But I believe that his thoughts about regional boards easily translate to his thoughts about where a regional bodies stands in the political culture. Karadzic tells us at page 27, and I'm quoting: "Regional boards would be a power structure above the municipal boards, instead of coordinating".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I apologise again. Let me start over. He tells us: "Regional boards would be a power structure above municipal boards, instead of coordinating boards, and it would cause a great deal of screaming and wailing in the municipal boards." We know from other witnesses that Karadzic's words about regional boards translated into his attitude and those of the upper echelons of the SDS about how they really felt about the ZOBK and then the ARK. Dobrivoje Vidic was an assemblyman, a deputy, to both the ZOBK and the ARK, and at pages 22954 through page 956, he talks about how from the beginning the ZOBK and the ARK was attacked by the upper echelons of the party. Not only did the ARK have to deal with the attacks from the upper echelons, but they had to deal with the municipalities, the presidents, as Ms. Korner so aptly put it yesterday, being the big fishes in the small ponds, not likely to give up power. And I remember what her statement was, and I differ with that, and I believe the evidence supports my position. I guess my point is this: When you have a party leader, someone with the power that Karadzic has, coming out and criticising, coming out against regional bodies, when you have municipality presidents who, in effect, see their power bases being threatened, I suggest to the Court that neither of them are going to give up that power. This institutional resistance by Mr. Karadzic and the upper echelons and by those strong presidents in the municipalities was one of the factors that the ARK was doomed from the very start. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I've talked a little bit about how Karadzic feels about regional bodies. Let me go back to February of 1992 to see how Mr. Karadzic feels about Mr. Brdjanin. Now, when we talk about February of 1992, it has to be placed in this context, because the Prosecution claims that this is -- that Mr. Brdjanin is an individual who has a close relationship with Karadzic, and in effect, they're working hand in hand and that the defendant is essential to that plan. In February, what we see is not just backdoor manoeuvring, backdoor quiet tongue-lashings in a party forum; what we see is full-blown, public humiliation and public ridicule of Brdjanin. And I suggest that this ridicule, this humiliation, is not something that's going to be forgotten by people in the party, people in power. Particularly those people that are beholden to Karadzic. It is something that further erodes any political legitimacy, any political credibility that Mr. Brdjanin might have. 25 February 1992 is an important date, and that is the meeting of the 8th session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is reflected -- the notes of it are reflected in Exhibit P33. And the Court will remember this because this is a time when Karadzic is reporting to the assembly on the status of talks in Lisbon and the discussions about the prospect of cantonisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the course of his speech, Mr. Karadzic is called off stage to take a phone call from Mr. Cutileiro, and to be informed that Mr. Izetbegovic has withdrawn from the agreement in principle. And it's known that Izetbegovic is withdrawing because of the talk of a -- the Serbian Assembly is about to adopt a constitution. When Karadzic comes back to this full assembly, he uses language that is harshly critical of Mr. Brdjanin, and it's not just critical, it starts to get humiliating. At page 43 of Exhibit P33, Karadzic reminds the attendees that they, the assembly, is a supreme power. At page 44, Karadzic vows not to allow five people with personal ambitions to destroy our chances. He then, in effect, calls out Mr. Brdjanin, asking him "do you have a better plan? Then you present it." This is what he says. And I'm quoting from page 71 now. "Neither Brdjo nor anyone else can act out of step with this assembly. They may, if they resign or until we reach a decision. But once we reach a decision, no one has a right to sabotage it." Now, the party leader has just attacked him in front of all his peers, and what does Mr. Brdjanin do? Mr. Brdjanin, on 27 February, is interviewed by a Sarajevo newspaper, and he's interviewed in a forum that he shares with Krajisnik. This interview is, again, 27 February 1992. It's reflected in Prosecutor's Exhibit 117. In this article, Brdjanin, it's reported, quoted as saying "Every Serbian deputy from the area of the Bosnian Krajina should have already resigned for failing to convey to the assembly the wishes of the people." He also says: "Well, you see, if the Serbian Assembly of BH does not feel this pulse of ours as it should, we shall put into actual practice our intention to declare the Serbian Republic of Krajina." All of this is being said with Krajisnik right there. Brdjanin continues: "So on 29 February if the Serbian Assembly of BH does not accommodate our request by then" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So on 29 February he says: "If the Serbian semi-by of BH does not accommodate our request by then, we shall proclaim the Serbian Republic of Krajina." And it's interesting because in an instance where the Prosecution claims the defendant is cooperating with them, hear in an openly public forum with the leading -- a leading figure of the SDS by his side, he has adopted a stance that's totally different from what the party says. And this stance, I suggest prompts the harshest criticism that comes a few days later. Actually, it's the next day. 28 February is a meeting of the SDS deputies' club, and at this meeting Karadzic is relentless in his criticism, but more importantly, his humiliation of Mr. Brdjanin. Can I see Exhibit P34. Your Honour, I'm handing an excerpt from that exhibit, P34, to the usher, and I'm going to be quoting from page 36. And I'd like to have that put on the ELMO. What does Karadzic say, again, in the presence of we would assume Mr. Brdjanin's peers and other party functionaries? He says the following: "We are in power, and we should exercise that power for the good of the people. We can and we must renounce everyone who refuses to work the way we have agreed. Brdjo and all the rest. When Brdjo appears somewhere, he's like a bomb. He blows up everything. Then he winks at him, and I won't allow it, as a psychiatrist and as the party leader. After an interruption, he continues. Karadzic humiliates him in front of his peers by saying: "He's crazy. He's not normal. He doesn't know what he can do and what he can't do." Now, I'd like the Chamber to ask themselves to be humiliated that way in front of your peers, how is that going to affect the peers, how is that going to affect the way that presidents of municipalities are going to look at Mr. Brdjanin after the party leadership has criticised him in the harshest way? But the criticism does not stop there. On the following day, the ARK Assembly meets. And we know from the evidence that the effort to form an independent Krajina is compromised. It's agreed. It's put aside. But that doesn't prevent Karadzic from continuing with the criticism. Because looking at Exhibit P35 -- and I'm sorry, Mr. Usher, I'm done -- which is an extract of the minutes of the ARK Assembly meeting of 29 February, there's criticism again of Mr. Brdjanin where he refers to those, including the defendant, who wanted an independent Krajina as being childish. Ms. Korner suggested that Dr. Donia said that the dispute between Pale and Banja Luka was over, that the meeting of 29 February healed all wounds. And I don't think it was advertent, but I think what Dr. Donia said was that, and I apologise, it's quoted in the brief but I don't have the quote here - that Dr. Donia claimed that the rift between Karadzic and the defendant was resolved, but he didn't say it was definitive. I think a reasonable deduction from the evidence is that Karadzic's criticism and public humiliation as well as Karadzic's public opposition to regional bodies has got to impact the way that people are going to view the defendant in the ARK. When the head of a party is so critical of Brdjanin, the very notion of a regional structure, surely that criticism has to impact, and it did impact, the way that people in the municipalities viewed the ARK, viewed the defendant. So where do we stand at the end of February? From the evidence there, it's clear that Karadzic doesn't think Brdjanin is very competent. He has called him crazy. He has called him a bomb. We know from Mr. Blagojevic, Boro Blagojevic, who testified that in the wake of this assembly meeting, that most of the municipality presidents gave their absolute support to the central powers. That's what Mr. Blagojevic says at transcript 21764. Now, what impact would the municipal leaders -- would this have on the municipal leaders, the big fish in the small pond? What is surprising is after this public humiliation, after Karadzic's speaking out against the regional bodies, that fact the Prosecution wants this Court to believe that in the span of about 65 days, 65 days being the time span between February 29th where Karadzic criticises those being for an independent Krajina as childish to May 5th, the date of the formation of the ARK Crisis Staff, that somehow, everyone is going to be willing to forget about this public criticism, that people are going to choose Brdjanin over Karadzic, and that the strong leaders within the local municipalities were going to hand over their power. Before I leave the events in February, I think it's also interesting to try to take a snapshot, if you will, of what is actually going on in the ARK. And I want to digress just a minute to talk about Section 16. Section 16 is something that the Prosecution has focussed on because it contains, as they say, a Defence provision, and they impute sinister connotations and sinister intentions to this. Your Honour, I suggest there's nothing sinister about this. In the former Yugoslavia, all people's defence, the TO, was the responsibility of the municipalities. And I suggest to the Court, in the ARK it was clear that all that was envisioned was cooperation regarding the municipal responsibilities regarding the ARK. And there is certainly support for this in the record. And I would cite the Court to Mr. Mirko Dejanovic's testimony at 23213. At that point, and I'm paraphrasing the question that was put to him, Was it unusual to have such a provision in the ARK statute? His answer: "This is not something unusual in our context. Even a company would have the same provision in its statute at the time, that it should take care of issues related to the coordination of the defence and so on and so forth." Well, let's look at what's logistically happening, and probably the better way to phrase it is not happening within the ARK. Brdjanin is the vice-president of the ARK, and we know from three witnesses who came and testified that in February of 1992, that the ARK is not functioning at all. We know this from -- the three witnesses are Jovica Radojko, from Bosanski Petrovac, we know from this Dobrivoje Vidic, from Prnjavor, and we know this from Mirko Dejanovic from Bosanski Novi. Yesterday, Ms. Korner talked about Mr. Radojko, and asked that this Court read the entirety of his testimony. I join in that request. I ask the Court to read it and to read it carefully because I think there are some very serious divergences between the way I interpret the testimony and the way Ms. Korner interprets it. But talking about the ARK, because in his duty as -- at Petrovac Radojko had to deal with the ARK. And at page 20093, that's 2-0-0-9-3, he is just appalled by the administrative disorganisation within the ARK. He told us at page 20012: When the ARK was formed, it was supposed to adopts the duties of government, but it was clear to them that it wouldn't do it. He says it rarely functioned if at all in the basic areas of economy, healthcare, education, pensions, health funds. In fact, he called it societal collapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, slow down again. I keep receiving notices here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I keep receiving noticed from Mr. Vujic, and everyone is on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko is also an interesting character because in dealing with the societal collapse of the ARK, we start to see a recurring theme; that is, when he needed something done, when he needed to go to Banja Luka, he didn't go to see Brdjanin. He went to go see Mr. Erceg. And the common theme, this theme that we see, is when people had problems within the ARK, they went to where the power was. And invariably, that power was not Mr. Brdjanin. We know from Mr. Radojko's testimony how the municipal leadership in Petrovac looked at the ARK. He testified, and I'll give the Court the page citations later on, because I bring those up when I talk about implementation, Mr. Radojko conveyed that the municipal leadership in effect thought that the ARK was a joke, that it wasn't doing anything to help them. And we know that this is something that's also echoed in effect by every municipality that's in the Sanska Unska group. We know in Bosanski Novi, from Mr. Mirko Dejanovic's testimony, he said "early on, they figured out that the ARK was not going to help them and that they had to fend for themselves." BT-95 said his municipality got nothing from the ARK and were in effect told to "fend for themselves." Sipovo, witness says: "Nothing came to them. They got nothing." Prnjavor, through Mr. Vidic, nothing came to them. The ARK may well have had some of the trappings of power in authority, but it didn't take members of the ARK Assembly very long to figure out what it was, that it was a farce, it was a sham, it was a body that had no real power. And what is interesting is invariably, witnesses talk about the ARK being impotent as a function of the fact of the ongoing dispute between the central powers and municipalities. We hear that from Mr. Sajic, BT-95. And I'll read his quote to the Court shortly. And Boro Blagojevic, who was present. I'd like to take a sidestep briefly because I broached Mr. Boro Blagojevic, I'd like to make a sidestep and talk about him and some things. The Prosecution claimed in effect during their summation that Mr. Blagojevic was a liar because of his testimony regarding the minutes, and then of course they then cite his testimony for the fact that the ARK was the lawful authority within the area. I understand that as a fact-finder, this Chamber can make credibility choices and can believe all, some, or none of what a witness has to testify. But I also think it's also fair to point out that during his testimony, he talked about crisis staffs, about how to the ARK the competency of the assembly was never transferred, that he called the crisis staff repeatedly an improvisation, and that it could not function. I apologise for that side -- aside, but I want to get back to the ARK Assembly, because I think it's important in determining and looking and trying to decide if there's any political legitimacy, any political credibility, any real power to the ARK, to consider the evidence that came from Mr. Vidic and Mr. Dejanovic. They both testified at trial that it didn't take them long to realise what a shell, what an empty promise, how no power resided in the ARK. And the Prosecution claims, makes the insinuation, that somehow, they got together and conjured up testimony. And I want the Court to consider that argument. Then I want you to look back and obviously use your experience and use your common sense and your recollection to remember just how they presented themselves, how Mr. Vidic and how Mr. Dejanovic presented themselves to the Court. Both of these men were well-educated individuals. Both of these men came in and dealt effectively with the cross-examination that they were presented. And yet, they're criticised because they both talk in very similar terms about the farcical nature of the ARK Assembly. The fact of the matter is these educated men saw through the ARK Assembly, saw that there was nothing to it, and they shouldn't be criticised for that. Their testimony was believable and credible. Well, let's talk about specifically what they said. Mr. Vidic, the Court will recall, was the former president of the Prnjavor Municipal Assembly. He was also a republican deputy. He outlined a number of factors which led him to quickly conclude this was not the ARK Assembly, a serious institution, that it was something totally devoid of any real power and authority. Vidic had long recognised something that I've talked about, that the upper echelons of the SDS were opposed to regional associations, and they were preventing the associations such as ZOBK and ARK have having any meaningful power. He tells us for example at page 22954, quoting from him testimony, "people attacked and undermined the initiative and kept it from being established." In a very similar vein, page 22956 to 57, he tells us: "But I do know that the members, the leaders of the SDS were not keen on that. You could see that at the first session in Celinac when there was a heated argument. The people who were involved in this argument were later to become very successful members of the SDS." Mr. Vidic, you'll recall, had a real interest in democracy and governance, but he tells the Court and told the Court at page 22964 that the ARK did not have any bodies that were subordinate to it. And as a result of that, he was not sure, and I'm quoting his testimony at 22969 - Vidic told the Court that he was not sure that "Krajina had the instruments of government whereby it would operate or act in the municipalities. Krajina could not force implementation because the municipalities had executive government, and Krajina did not have executive government." In his view, as a result, many municipalities did not implement decisions of the ARK Assembly. No sanctions were ever imposed. And what's interesting is what his recurring assessment of the ARK was. He has called it "nothing." Proforma. It had no power. No jurisdiction over anything. He told the Court "we just had meetings at the time because there were no instruments to use." And in a very, very apt summary of the ARK, he says, I'm quoting from page 23102: "They had no influence over anything. They were merely expressing their support for someone or the other. They might as well have been an ordinary association. That's at least the way it looked." We remember from his testimony, and I'm sure Your Honours do, how critical he was of the lack of protocol and procedure. And before I read the next passage, and I hate to keep harping on political legitimacy, but if there's anything that shows just how totally devoid of legitimacy that the ARK Assembly was it's the following passage. He is being -- he is asked about protocol. And I'm quoting now from page 23078. "It was ridiculous. There was no protocol. There were no accreditation. Nobody knew who was invited. And because I did not agree with this kind of work, to work without the rules of procedure, and Mr. Brdjanin probably remembers that, he said, well, why are you bothered by that? I know that I was quite literally thrown out of the session. It was held in a hall which was twice as small as this one here. I was kicked out, and my driver remained there, and he laughed later on, saying that he, in fact, passed some of the decisions. I've refused to go there because I couldn't do anything." Vidic in that statement pointed out in effect how it was possible for literally anyone off the street to come in and give a speech. Mr. Dejanovic a criticised because in effect he agreed with it. In effect he saw the very same thing. Dejanovic told the Court at page 23156, and remember Mr. Dejanovic was testifying in English at this stage, about people coming in off the streets. "It was like Hyde park." And there he's referring to Speaker's Corner obviously. "Everyone could enter. Everyone could have a speech. It was a very unserious job. It was really funny, let's say, because there is no minutes. There is no rules about proceeding, these minutes." Another thing in their eyes, at least in Mr. Vidic's eyes, which affected the legitimacy of the ARK Assembly was the concern that he had about the way that Mr. Boro Blagojevic handled the documents. Those are cited extensively in our brief, but I bring up these points about Mr. Radojko, Mr. Vidic, Mr. Dejanovic and their views of the ARK Assembly, because these are all three individuals with important ties to municipalities. All three of them told the Court that as an institution, the ARK was not working, that it had at best limited legitimacy. They also told us, at least Mr. Vidic did, that it was opposed by the SDS upper echelons. That's talking about municipalities. It's good now to talk about Karadzic and his relationship to the municipalities. When the head of a political party is so openly critical of Mr. Brdjanin, when he's so openly critical of these regional structures, that has got to affect, I've said, the way that people view Mr. Brdjanin and the ARK. The upper echelons, Mr. Karadzic did what they could do to hamstring it, and now I want to talk a little bit about the municipalities, how they viewed what was going on. And because I'm going to quote a protected witness, if I could, Your Honour, I'd like to go very briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In their brief, in their submissions earlier this week, the Prosecution often cited the Court to BT-104 as being a well-placed Serb witness. What I'd like to do is talk about another well-placed Serb witness, someone who was in a position to monitor what was going on and take, if you will, the pulse at this time. And that is Milorad Dodik. And he was questioned about the relationship between the municipalities and in the context here, the ARK Crisis Staff. And this is what he said. I'm quoting to the Court from page 20520. "In many municipalities, there were strong, local persons who at given points in time and in certain activities had full independence. This assessment is based on conversations with people who were familiar with the situation." He continues: "I know that it is only local people who were of key importance and in other places, too. They were autonomous. I think they had stronger links to the top echelons of government then - Karadzic at the time - rather than the crisis staff and other regional groups." Among those he expressly mentioned, Mr. Dodik, were Gojko Klickovic and Miroslav Vjestica, I have yet to get that right, but the two gentlemen from Krupa. He referenced Simo Drljaca in Prijedor, and he referenced a Mr. Rasula in Sanski Most. As we get into the spring of 1992, I think it's clear from what I've put in our written submissions and what I've presented to the Court today that in effect, the ARK was a farce, a sham, with no real power, that there was both institutional resistance coming to it from Sarajevo, then Pale, and then the municipalities, and that these forces did, in effect, obstructed, resisted, and nullified any power that the ARK might have. I'm going to talk about the ARK Crisis Staff obviously, but I think here is a good point, again, to take a step back and talk about the description of life in Banja Luka in the spring of 1992. Because there is an important divergence between what I'll call international witnesses and what -- and the non-Serb population. I'm not suggesting that life was roses in Banja Luka at all, but I think there are some critical differences that need to be pointed out. Mr. Krzic who the Court remembers was one of the very, very first witnesses in this case constantly refer to the fact that Banja Luka was a ghetto for the non-Serbs. Other witnesses claim, came in and testified that ethnic cleansing and genocide was taking place. The Court remembers the testimony of BT-20, (redacted) (redacted) by Mr. Ackerman, "Was Banja Luka a ghetto for the non-Serbs?" He disagreed [Realtime transcript read in error "agreed"] with that. The Court, I'd also refer the Court to the conversation, the exchange between Mr. Krzic and Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was in closed session, Your Honour, this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for pointing that out. Madam Registrar, we need to block -- we are going to block it. No major harm done. But try to avoid mentioning names of witnesses who --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just so that I can tell the Court what -- and I don't mean to get into a long discussion about this. It was my instructions, my understanding from Mr. Ackerman, as long as I do not do anything that could even remotely reveal who this individual was. But I understand the Court's admonition, and I'll take that in due course. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, I agree with that, and in two cases I referred to some testimony without -- because it didn't identify. But I think this particular question and answer would because he was the only one -- are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. But I think I would agree with you. utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I will, Your Honour. And I apologise.

utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. Cunningham. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Before we go, there is an error in the transcript, at page 66, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I thought I said that he disagreed with that notion.
