utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At all. In talking, I think, another passage that might be instructive for the Court is the exchange between Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Krzic which appears at page 1788 to 1789. This is a passage where Mr. Krzic is being cross-examined about his claim of ethnic cleansing occurring in Banja Luka. And I'm paraphrasing now, but what happens is during this exchange, Mr. Ackerman talks to him, Mr. Krzic, about the fact that Mr. Krzic had talked to the reporter, Roy Gutman, that he had spoken with him apparently in his home, and Mr. Krzic, if my recollection is correct, agreed that Mr. Gutman was a responsible journalist. Mr. Krzic was then confronted with Mr. Gutman's articles in Newsday and was specifically asked whether he agreed with Mr. Gutman's writings, which said "until now, Banja Luka, the principal city in northern Bosnia, has largely been spared the terror tactics of ethnic cleansing, the practice of emptying territories of unwanted ethnic groups." And of course, Mr. Krzic agreed with the representations or the writings of someone he called a responsible journalist. And getting back to my point, Your Honour, again, life for everyone in Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992 was difficult. But I'd like to cite the Court, to remind the Court of the testimony of Milenko Savic. Mr. Savic was a Serb officer, police officer from Prnjavor, an individual that had no political ties because he felt as a professional police officer it was appropriate, necessary, for him not to join any political parties. The Court will recall from his testimony that he was in Prnjavor up until March or April of 1992, that he was then transferred to Banja Luka where he did white-collar crime investigation. And one of the points that was brought out during his testimony is that during his travels throughout the Krajina in 1991 and 1992, the safest place, the safest places to be were Banja Luka and Celinac. That can be found at page 22.390 through 92. And it's also confirmed by some of the charts obviously that Ms. Korner showed yesterday. I want to switch gears, if you will, and talk about something else now that is connected to something that Ms. Korner represented -- excuse me, that she talked about this morning. And that has to deal with the international individuals, the international organisations that come to Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992. Ms. Korner's argument, in effect, is "they really don't matter because who would put Brdjanin -- who would present Brdjanin to these individuals?" She also argued yesterday that with respect to the non-Serb population, and this might have been Monday when she quoted a witness saying, in effect, that they felt it would be fruitless to go to Mr. Brdjanin because of his speeches. The fact of the matter is that the international organisations, their representatives who came to Banja Luka, in effect went to where the power was, and invariably, the power, the authority, was someone other than Mr. Brdjanin. Judge, Your Honours, I don't remember with respect to the military monitors whether that was in closed session or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. We've discussed this in detail in our brief, but I do want to bring out some points. The European Community military monitors came to Banja Luka throughout 1991 and 1992. And they went to see Mr. Radic invariably, invariably. And it's important to note that at this stage that Mr. Radic is not just talking about matters that are limited to the municipality of Banja Luka; but in essence, he is talking about Krajina-wide issues. And I think it's important, if I could look at Exhibit 61 -- 615. The print on this is very, very small, Your Honour. I'm not going to put it on the ELMO. I can read a very, very short passage. To put this exhibit in its proper context, Exhibit P1615, is a report dated 20 April 1992. It's done by one of the monitors, and it references a visit to Mayor Radic of Banja Luka. And I think this is important because the date, as we recognise, 20 April 1992, is after the first week of April, after the appearance of the SOS. And what does this exhibit say? On the second page, in very small print, it says, talking about Mr. Radic, "We feel that he's the most realistic, flexible, and workable basis for future agreements - referring to Radic. We feel that since he - Radic - is receptive to this and since he is a potentially important figure in the formation of politics to be, it is significant and may be a good basis for future agreements, negotiations on the whole problem." Now, to be fair, there is one notation of Mr. Brdjanin being present at a meeting with the ECMM, and that is a meeting with a group of six or seven other individuals in early February in Celinac Municipality. But that is in effect the only mention of him from the military monitors. I'd like to go talk about a witness that testified in closed session, so if we could go into private session so I can briefly discuss him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to have a short break, resuming at 10 minutes to 1.00, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, during the break, I was admonished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Severely, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, they were very friendly with me, but they suggested that I take it from 33 down to 16, so... With that in mind, I'll try. When we left off, Your Honours, we were talking about the internationals and their search, if you will, for the power, their assessment of the power in the Krajina. I have been informed that the witness I'm going to talk about next was not a protected witness, although he's related to an international organisation. And that's Mr. Krudja. The Court remembers obviously what -- his position. The Court obviously remembers where he was stationed; that is, right across the river from Novi. And in his time in this area, although he was dealing with an area that was a part of the ARK, he had no contacts, no reference, heard no mention of Radoslav Brdjanin. What is interesting is, the records reflects, that he did receive a phone call or a message that was taken from a Mr. Kupresanin, the mayor of Banja Luka. But more importantly, when this well-educated, well-trained, and experienced individual gave his assessment of where the authority lied, he said that in the area where he was working, the presidents of the municipalities showed a complete deference to Knin, and they -- he called that the "the centre for the coordination of authority." Another international that visited the Banja Luka area or the Krajina was Mr. Mazowietski, that came in August 1992. Again, no mention of Mr. Brdjanin. Reflected in BT-94's diary is reference to the visit of General Nambiar, the head of UNPROFOR when he came to Banja Luka. And interestingly enough, when he came to Banja Luka, he did not meet with Mr. Brdjanin, the so-called master of life and death in the Krajina. I've talked about the international organisations. On a similar note, let me talk now about the charitable organisations. And this Court heard of the efforts of Caritas and Merhamet. And I'd like to go into private session, because I'm going to reference someone who I believe testified with full protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to the Court about Exhibit 256. And if I could have the usher place the second page of this exhibit up on the ELMO. This exhibit deals with, among other things, the provision of Merhamet aid within the Krajina. And this exhibit, P256, is a summary of a meeting held between various representatives of the non-Serb community. It's interesting for several things, one of which is that the meeting is not held with Mr. Brdjanin, the so-called master of life and death. But the meeting is held with General Talic. And I believe the date on this is June 22nd, during the time that the ARK Crisis Staff is still in operation, during a time, if you will, as the Prosecution claims, there was close coordination and cooperation between Mr. Brdjanin and the military and security organs. But what's interesting is Mr. Talic, General Talic, in dealing with their complaints, where does he direct these individuals to go? He directs them, and if I'm correct it's on page 2, "Muslims should contact the crisis staff of Banja Luka Municipal Assembly and request visits to the collection centres and concentration camps and everything else connected with this." Again, further indication of where the actual power lay. In a related point to this, Your Honour, and thank you, Mr. Usher, I'm done, and it's something we didn't raise in our brief but I think it's something that is equally applicable to this point, during the trial the Court received a number of exhibits that were in effect letters written by Bishop Komarica. These letters were written on behalf of his parishioners, written in an attempt to improve the conditions, if you will, make life better. While there are a number of letters directed to individuals I've talked about before, Mr. Radic, Mr. Zupljanin, there is no letter directed to Mr. Brdjanin. And this is some evidence of the fact that despite the fact Mr. Brdjanin held the title of vice-president of the ARK Assembly, and later president of the ARK Crisis Staff, he was not recognised by many circles as being an individual with power. I'd like to now talk about the formation of the ARK Crisis Staff. And obviously, we see it in our dreams, and we know that the ARK Crisis Staff was formed on the first part of May, 5 May 1992. In our written submissions to the Court, we talked about -- we referenced the legality of the ARK. And when we make these arguments, Your Honour, obviously this is not a challenge, if you will, a legal challenge claiming, you know, somehow that the ARK was illegal. It's phrased in this context or put in this context: The legality of the ARK Crisis Staff was questioned by and reflected in exhibits by members of the upper echelons of the SDS. The perfect example of the way that the upper echelons of the SDS, the republican officials, felt about the ARK is reflected in one of the entries in BT-94's diary. That diary, obviously, is Exhibit 2326. And in that, the witness refers to a Glas article on 6 July 1992; again, the ARK Crisis Staff is in operation. And the statement is attributed to the republican minister of defence, the minister of Defence, the Court remembers, is Mr. Subotic. And this is what the article says. In quoting Mr. Subotic, Glas reported. "On the occasion, that the establishment of crisis staffs did not have a legal founding. It was simply a case of copying something that the Ustasha created and introduced into the Croatian practice." Now, that's an important point especially when it's considered in conjunction with one of the things that Mr. Blagojevic said, and that is at the ARK Crisis Staff meeting, people came in and openly challenged the legality of the ARK Crisis Staff. And this gets back to the point that I have been making or trying to make throughout, and that is when you have the republican leadership, someone like Mr. Subotic criticising it in the press, when you have attendees questioning the very legality of the ARK, how much legitimacy does it have? I submit that it has no legitimacy, no credibility, no power. I want to talk now about the members of the ARK Crisis Staff. The Prosecution has claimed repeatedly throughout the case that the very composition of the ARK Crisis Staff, the members, if you will, the corps members, and their positions ensured that the ARK's directives would be followed. I'm going to submit to the Court if you look at these corps members, if you look at their statements and/or their attendance records, that we're going to see a familiar theme. That is, much like the ARK Assembly members who came, Mr. Vidic and Mr. Dejanovic, realised that the ARK Assembly had no power, it didn't take long for members, the corps members, if you will, of the ARK Crisis Staff to determine that this was a body with no power, no real authority. The first witness to start with is Mr. Radic. Obviously, we all know, president of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, the mayor, if you will, of the most populated, the most influential municipality in the ARK. He quit going to the meetings rather quickly because he felt one, it was unorganised; two, didn't feel with serious issues; and most importantly, three, felt it was a waste of time. Mr. Erceg is the man who with the stroke of his pen created it; yet the witnesses said that his attendance was at best one-third of the time. Mr. Sajic came in and testified and described Mr. Erceg's attitude towards the crisis staff. He said, Sajic did, "he did not see the crisis staff as a body that was superior to him. He had no respect for this body as a superior body, and he, Erceg, believed that his duty was to run the municipality and to rally behind the republican structures." Now, that's what one witness says about the, if you will, the founder of the ARK Crisis Staff. Now, how much legitimacy does that add to this organisation? Milorad Sajic obviously was a member, and he was surprised when he was a member. And he told the Prosecution in interview and he repeated it in Court that he was surprised to find out that he ever was the vice-president of the ARK Crisis Staff. He didn't know that until well after the fact. He also told the Court that he had other business that prevented him from attending, and he didn't go. And when you consider these attendance records, it raises a question at least in my mind and I hope it raises the same question in your mind, and that is, if this is the highest body in the Krajina, why is it that these members come and go when they please, why is it, if you don't come, there is no sanction? Why is it, like Zoran Jokic, the air force pilot, when you decide you're not coming any more, no one even bothers to call you up and find out your reason? The Prosecution's answer to this is, of course, the sinister approach. These witnesses, Your Honours, they argue, are simply trying to distance themselves. I submit an equally permissible deduction from this evidence is, much like the municipal -- much like the ARK Assembly members, it didn't take these individuals long to realise what a joke, what a farce this was. General Talic, we know, the evidence is, attended at best one meeting, and then he directed a representative to attend the meetings and report. And much is read into the fact of this by the Prosecution, but one of their very own witnesses and because I'm unsure if this witness testified -- his name is used throughout the record. So to be sure, can I ask to go into private session very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I thank Ms. Korner for the assistance, and I

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Much is made of the fact that Vujnovic was directed to attend these meetings. But as we'll see when I talk about the military aspect of this case, Osman Selak saw absolutely nothing wrong with that. But what is interesting, if we look at some of the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff, it shows how utterly powerless it is because what I'd like to do is show the Court a couple of the conclusions. If I could see 15 May 1992. Apparently, I don't have that one. I apologise for making the usher come over here. But I do have it written verbatim. In 15 May 1992, a conclusion is delivered, and it reads as follows: "Talks should be held with General Talic about calling up and assigning military conscripts on 20 and 21 May 1992." Now, obviously Mr. Talic, General Talic, didn't bother to show up because if we look at the conclusion from 22 May, we see the following passage, the following conclusion, number 4. "In view of the present poor coordination between the Crisis Staff and the newly established army, the VRS, mandatory attendance of General Talic, or a person designated by him, is requested." I'm done with that exhibit. But it's kind of interesting. Mandatory attendance is not requested, mandatory attendance is demanded. And the fact of the matter that they couldn't do that is further indication of just how woefully inadequate, how woefully powerless this body was. If you look at the citations in our brief as to the attendance of the corps members, to put it mildly, it's woeful. Mr. Blagojevic just testified that after a while they quit coming. And again, the reason I suggest that happens is these are individuals who quickly saw that it was a joke, that it was not a serious institution. It was, as Predrag Radic called it, a waste of time. We know from the evidence that presidents of the municipalities were in attendance. And I'm going to submit that the evidence shows the following: Much as the ARK Assembly members saw it for what it was, much as the corps members saw it for what it was, the municipality presidents saw it as a body that could not help them. And there is a quote that is very, very indicative of it that comes from a witness who testified in closed session, so we need to go into private session with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session once more, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This, again, was echoed by Mr. Dejanovic who the Court recalls was a member of the crisis staff in Bosanski Novi, and he testified that again, we realised that we had to help ourselves because we would not get any help from the ARK. That's at page 23156. Now, what's interesting is much like the corps members felt like they didn't have to attend meetings and if they had something else in the works, that they wouldn't go, individuals from the crisis staffs, the municipal crisis staffs felt the same way. And rather -- I'm just going to direct the Court to three witnesses and to some citations that confirm the fact that they didn't believe that they had to attend, that many times they didn't bother to send a replacement. And these citations are as follows: BT-103 at page 19930; BT-95, 19581 through 82; BT-92, 19898. During the course of our presentation of evidence, we brought to the Court just how woefully lacking the ARK Crisis Staff and the ARK was in, if you will, the trappings of authority. And that's important, because it again points to the lack of legitimacy that the institution had. And it also points out the fact that they were basically, if you will, a pawn between the municipalities and the upper echelons of the SDS. When Mr. Blagojevic and other witnesses testified that the ARK, the ARK Crisis Staff, didn't have its own offices, that it was forced to borrow space from Banja Luka Municipality, that there were only two paid employees for this institution that is supposed to be in control of the Krajina. And those two paid employees were Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Kupresanin. And of course, that stands in stark contrast to what was the number of employees at Banja Luka Municipality which was in the neighbourhood, one witness testified, 350 to 380. And I think someone else testified maybe as much as 600. And the reason that the ARK was treated, as we call in the States as the red-headed stepchild, was not really given the time of day was because Mr. Kasagic the president of the executive council in Banja Luka never supported the crisis staff and never lent it any support. Now, Mr. Blagojevic talked about how they didn't even have the simple things. Audiorecorders, anything to take minutes. And he took a lot of heat in that from the Prosecution about the minutes and obviously that caused the Court some concern as to whether or not there were really minutes. But what's interesting, and I'm going to find an exhibit -- I'm reading from Exhibit 247, which is one of the Sanska Unska documents, this is the one -- the latter one dated 14 June. And the Court recalls that this is the document where this group is making demands. It's interesting because one of the demands that they make is on the second page, under letter C, and they demand "in the future, all sessions of the ARK Crisis Staff shall be recorded on tape and the minutes taken by several clerks." That suggests at least to me that maybe there weren't any minutes being taken. But that kind of sidetracks from my points, which is you have an institution that didn't have its own office space, an institution that couldn't even get a tape recorder, an institution that didn't have a stamp and had to borrow a stamp. All that points to, again, the fact that this was not a serious institution. But there's one -- there's one ARK Crisis Staff conclusion that really attests to how impotent this entity was. If I could see 22 May. We know from the evidence that the ARK Crisis Staff or the ARK tried to get offices. And they issued a conclusion on 22 May to that effect. And I want the Court to consider this conclusion in the light of the Prosecution's arguments that they made in their brief. Paragraph 341, the Prosecution argues: "These conclusions were orders, obedience was mandatory." Paragraph 97: Prosecution argues: "Instructions were followed and witnesses were of a view that had they not complied with the instructions they would be replaced." If I could have the usher place this on the ELMO, I'm going to draw the Court's attention to the very first conclusion of 22 May 1992. The decision reads, the conclusion to be fair: "By 30 May 1992, the second floor of the employment bureau is to be fully prepared to house the offices of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Nothing happened. They never moved. More importantly, there has never been any evidence as far as I can recall, and I'm sure if there's anyone who can recall, it's you Judge Agius, but I don't believe there was any evidence that said they even started to make preparations for this move. And thank you, Mr. Usher. If there's something that points out how impotent this entity was, this entity couldn't even fend for itself to acquire the basic essentials it needs as an administrative body. Is -- if this body cannot even fend for itself, how can it be said that they directed or instigated or ordered other entities, other municipalities, other structures within the Krajina? While we're on the crisis staff, I want to talk and answer some of the arguments that have been made by the Prosecution that deal with what I call the self-congratulatory phrases and decisions passed by the ARK Crisis Staff. Can I see Exhibit 182, and then 9 May. Start with that one first. Thank you. Four days after the crisis staff is formed, 9 May 1992, we see Exhibit 182, and this should be a decision. Four days after their very formation, the ARK Crisis Staff feels it's important to tell everyone that "all the decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are binding for all the municipalities. "Objections to or appeals against decrees from the previous paragraph will not delay their implementation." It seems to me that if this is the highest body in the land, that that should have been readily evident to everyone in the land on 5 May. But four days later, they have to adopt that decision. If we can put on now the decision of 9 May 1992. It's a -- it's a conclusion. Should be the other one I gave. This comes out of P227. Again, four days after its inception, the following conclusion: "Decisions adopted by the war staff are to be strictly respected in all public and economic organisations." Okay. Thank you. You would think maybe, after four days and after these conclusions, that maybe someone was getting the point that supposedly we are the highest authority in the land. But apparently, someone must not have been listening very closely because two days later, on 11 May, they feel compelled to issue another -- this is a conclusion from 11 May, where they say "the work of the crisis staff of the autonomous region is given full support." Not really sure what that means, but they are constantly having to proclaim themselves to be, if you will, the highest law in the land. But the important thing is no one's listening because on 18 May, they feel compelled to issue another conclusion where they tell us, at 18 May, conclusion 2, and this is at page 21 of Exhibit P227, the English version, that "the crisis staffs are now the highest authority in the municipalities." But the message that I talked about on 9 May about the crisis staff decisions being binding still is not getting through, because 26 May, there's this conclusion: "The work of the crisis staff has absolute support since it's now the highest organ of authority in the Krajina as the assembly cannot function due to objective and subjective circumstances." It has to repeat that "decisions of the crisis staff are binding for all crisis staffs in the municipality." And then they tell in the decision that decisions will be submitted for verification as soon as practicable. It's interesting because in the three weeks that they have been in existence, they feel, the ARK Crisis Staff feels compelled to issue three different conclusions or decisions where they have to proclaim themselves the highest authority, and that their decisions need to be respected. Now, shouldn't it be obvious, or are people ignoring them? And I submit to you it's the latter. And the reason I do that is because we know of the struggle between the upper echelons, the big fish in the small ponds at the municipality, and I submit to the Court the municipalities realised just as the assembly members did, just as the corps members did, just as the presidents did, that this institution really has no authority. What's interesting is how the ARK tries to resolve that problem, and that's in their amendment or their purported amendment of Article 35, which is the Court remembers is the provisions dealing for how decisions would be adopted in the municipalities. On 15 June 1992, the decision is issued. It states: "Paragraph 2 of Article 35 of the ARK Statute is hereby amended to read: `The decisions and conclusions must be respected by the municipality.'" I submit to the Court that the reason they had to do this was they were ignored in the municipality. These municipal presidents didn't feel like they were compelled to answer, to implement everything that came. I want to talk about the municipalities now and the notion of implementation. And I want to recite to the Court a couple of points made by the Prosecutor in their briefs. Paragraph 181, they argue that the regional crisis staff had a great deal of authority over municipal bodies notwithstanding occasion complaints or incidents of revolt and put into effect all the major decisions which were designed to create an ethnically pure state. Paragraph 414 of the Prosecution brief: "Municipal leaders who on the evidence did accept orders and directions from the accused in his capacity as president of the ARK Crisis Staff..." I'm going to talk about the notion of implementation now, and this is going to require some discussion about witnesses from the municipalities. But it's interesting to start with the report of Patrick Treanor. When we talk about implementation, because although there were a number of decisions and conclusions, the evidence is overwhelmingly clear that the vast overwhelming majority of these were never, ever implemented in the respective municipalities. That is a point that Mr. Treanor conceded even before he got to the witness stand because paragraph 186 of his report says as follows: "The available documentary evidence would not suffice to prove or to reasonably infer a scheme of systematic and mandatory implementation of all of Brdjanin's enactments by municipal bodies." That's at paragraph 186. And I see you nodding your head, Your Honour, because I remember you questioned him on the next paragraph as well. Paragraph 187 says: "The available documentary evidence is more compelling in the above-mentioned critical areas, disarmament, dismissals, and resettlement, regardless of the precise state of authority of Brdjanin, his enactments were, in fact, implemented in these critical -- for these three critical purposes. In these three areas, the available documentary evidence indicates the municipal institutions acted either directly or prompted by Brdjanin or in a way concurrent and consistent with his policies." Earlier in the report, Treanor had tried to back up his arguments about implementation, and I'm going to cite from paragraph 165, he says in that paragraph: "The overall coordination of evidence available on implementation of ARK Crisis Staff enactments in the 13 relevant municipalities would provide an estimate of 11.9 per cent of provable implementation." Stated another way, in the light most favourable to the Prosecution, that means that there was an 88 per cent rate of non-implementation. And I'm going to submit to the Court, there's a problem even with Treanor's 12 per cent rate of provable implementation, and that's going to require the Court to again look at his notion, Mr. Treanor's notion, of cumulative evidence of implementation. It's described in paragraph 164 of his report, and for the Court his report is P2353. He says the following: "Cumulative evidence of implementation. The decisions or actions at the local level coincide with one or more items passed by the ARK Crisis Staff. The ARK Crisis Staff is not mentioned in the municipal decision. The action at the lower level could have been caused by authorities other than the ARK Crisis Staff itself, RS, SDS, MUP, CSB, and VRS. The evidence seems to be inefficient to establish a direct causal link between the local level and the ARK Crisis Staff. The evidence, rather, indicates parallel, concurrent action or common purpose between the local bodies and the ARK Crisis Staff." I submit to the Court by its very definition, these events, this concurrent, cumulative evidence of implementation should be dropped from any notion of provable implementation because by his own admission, there's no causal connection. If you do that, the rate of non-implementation rises from 88 per cent to 96 per cent. I want to now talk about the municipalities and implementation and in the notion of implementation in the municipalities. I'll start with Banja Luka. We know from our remarks, my remarks, as well as the written submissions that the local officials in Banja Luka took a dim view of the ARK Crisis Staff. There is an exhibit, DB292, a Glas newspaper article where Mr. Kasagic, the president of the executive board, is talking. And he in this article talks about how he is against the ARK Crisis Staff taking power. When Mr. Radic came and testified, he told the Court that Mr. Kasagic opposed the crisis staff because he was afraid it would interfere with Banja Luka's policies. That same article, DB292, also quotes Mr. Kasagic as saying: "The smaller municipalities were not putting into effect its decisions." When Mr. Radic was here for that week, he was, of course, questioned about crisis staff decisions. And he was emphatic that they did not implement any decisions from the ARK Crisis Staff, and even challenged the Prosecutor to show them an instance. And the Prosecutor didn't, and I suggest that's because they were aware of what Mr. Treanor said in his report, and this is paragraph 164 from 2354. Treanor states the following with respect to Banja Luka: "There is little evidence of implementation by the municipal crisis staff of regional crisis staff enactments. Six instances. The Official Gazette of Banja Luka Municipality does not show specific indications of linkage to the ARK Crisis Staff, nevertheless the regional crisis staff having its seat in Banja Luka may have been in a position to have direct influence over this municipality. Predrag Radic, the president of the Banja Luka crisis staff, was also a member of the ARK Crisis Staff." Mr. Radic's testimony, Mr. Treanor's assessment of implementation was confirmed when Mr. Cvijic came to testify. Mr. Cvijic, the Court will recall, was the secretary of the municipal assembly. He told the Court and I'm quoting from page 2142 and it carries over to 13, that the ARK Crisis Staff never ordered anything to the municipality of Banja Luka. It never proposed any issues for discussion, nothing that pertained to the work of the crisis staff was ever discussed by the municipality. The Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka never had any such orders instituted to them. Just to make sure the record is clear the complete citation is 21412 carrying over to 413. Your Honours, I see I have about five minutes. I'm about to go into the Sanska Unska group, and with your permission I'd like to start that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I continue presuming that you should be able to conclude tomorrow between you and Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know that we have much choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. But the thing is this, no, let's put it like this. You conceded an hour and a half to Ms. Korner, so I think it's only fair on my part to ask what the position looks like at this present moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we can finish tomorrow. I think we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We appreciate it. Basically, I think we can use the next five minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We shall now give two oral decisions as anticipated during yesterday's sitting, both decisions relate to a corresponding Defence motion. Our first oral decision relates to a confidential motion to strike the Prosecution's final brief filed by the accused on April 16. It has been decided first, although it was the last one to be filed, because if it is successful then the other motion becomes moot automatically since Appendix C is an integral part of the Prosecution final brief. The Prosecution final brief was filed on April 5. In support of his motion, the accused makes the following submissions. The Prosecution's final brief contains countless misstatements of fact and improper footnote citations that are designed to mislead or have the effect of misleading the Trial Chamber. In addition, the Prosecution attempts to interject factual findings from both Stakic and Plavsic cases into this case, a practice which according to him is highly improper. The accused submits that these shortcomings are improper and unprofessional enough to warrant the striking of the Prosecution's final brief. The Prosecution's final brief, according to the accused, takes answers totally out of context and fails to provide the complete nature of a witness testimony. In addition, it consistently mis-cited, directed the reader to pages which do not support the assertion made, and at times directed us to testimony and/or exhibits which do not exist or are wholly inapplicable. The accused then gave several examples in support of his arguments asserting that these showed a pattern in the brief that can only lead to one conclusion; namely, that the Prosecution was deliberately trying to mislead the Chamber. Finally, the accused submitted that in paragraph 445 of the final brief, although the Prosecution notes that the factual findings of the Stakic case in no way bind this Chamber, it nonetheless turns around and injects those factual findings into their arguments suggesting that this Court adopt in toto the findings of another Chamber when the witness was not subjected to cross-examination in this case, and this Chamber did not have the opportunity to see and assess the witness's demeanour and credibility. He pointed out that this improper use of the Stakic judgement appears in various paragraphs of the brief. The accused also submitted that the Prosecution seek to do likewise in paragraph 571 where in footnote 1072 they seek to inject testimony from the Plavsic, Biljana Plavsic case. The Prosecutor filed her response on April 19, making several submissions, chief of which are the following: The motion is an effort to impugn the integrity of the Prosecution and prevent the Trial Chamber from hearing argument which may weigh against the accused. The Prosecution readily concedes that on rereading the final trial brief, there are some inadvertent errors in the facts and/or citations contained therein. The Prosecution points out that the reason for footnoting assertions of fact and law is to give the Trial Chamber the opportunity to check the accuracy of these assertions. Not just the Trial Chamber, but also the accused. The Prosecution is categoric that none of the errors which exist are intentional, and no part of any filing by the Prosecution is intended to mislead. It is also submitted that much of the motion is merely more argument on the facts. There are other submissions, particularly with regard to the alleged interjection of factual findings from the Stakic and the Biljana Plavsic, the allegation is denied, and the Prosecution points out that they cited the Stakic trial judgement principally to address the accused's own suggestion from the Rule 98 bis stage; namely, that the Stakic trial judgement findings on genocide somehow preclude a genocide conviction in this case. In addition, the Prosecution also purports to make clear that the Trial Chamber is not being asked to adopt these factual findings from Stakic and Plavsic, but rather to decide on the case of the evidence presented, and if the Trial Chamber chooses to completely disregard the various references relevant, relevant references, then it can easily do so. The Trial Chamber fully understands and appreciates that mistakes in the statement and in the description of facts or in references sometimes do happen and sometimes do happen inadvertently and unavoidably, especially in long and complicated cases like the present one, where the Trial Chamber and the parties have to deal with thousands of documents containing thousands and thousands of pages, plus thousands of pages of transcript of evidence in these proceedings. The presumption is, and short of proof to the contrary, remains that such mistakes are made inadvertently, sometimes also the result of negligence. They can, of course, exceptionally be made intentionally, but then the supposition, whoever resorts, the supposition is that whoever resorts to such egregious and despicable tactics does so in the foolish expectation, or assumption for that matter, that whoever is ultimately called to decide the case will take for granted every submissions made as made without due verification. The supposition would also be that opposing counsel, too, is incompetent or irresponsible enough not to bother to check on the submissions and references made to the Chamber or to take such submissions for granted. In reality, however, it's practically impossible to envisage such a scenario. As conceded by the Prosecution itself, there are some mistakes in the final brief, but there is absolutely no basis for the assertion by the accused that any of these "countless misstatements of fact and improper footnote citations" contained in the Prosecution's final brief were or are designed to mislead the Trial Chamber. The accused also contends that these misstatements of fact and improper footnote citations have the effect of misleading the Trial Chamber nonetheless. The accused may rest assured that the Trial Chamber will not allow itself to be misled by anything or anyone and can therefore put his mind at rest or at ease without deciding for the Trial Chamber what weight, what value to give to the various pleadings filed by the Prosecution. With regard to the alleged improper interjection of factual findings from other Chambers, the Trial Chamber finds the explanation given by the Prosecution satisfactory; however, the Trial Chamber points out that it will treat these references as submitted by the Prosecution and not by way of adopting the relative findings as feared by the accused. This case will be decided on the evidence presented in the case -- in this case, and not on any other. This motion, therefore, that is the accused's motion of April 16 2004 to strike the Prosecution's final brief, is rejected. Our second decision disposes of a confidential motion filed by the accused on April 12th, 2004, seeking to strike Appendix C of the Prosecutor's final brief. The accused moved this Court to strike Appendix C of the Prosecutor's final brief, bringing forward the following arguments: The Prosecution is attempting to introduce new evidence before the Chamber in the form of a revised version of a purported section of a previously admitted exhibit. According to the Prosecution, Appendix C represents a revised version of Section 5, V, of addendum report by expert Patrick Treanor, Exhibit 3253. That's not correct. I think it's a mistake there. According to the table of contents to the Treanor addendum report, Section V consists of nine pages of text, and this is in the submission of the accused completely different from the document called Appendix C which is 65 pages spreadsheet. If the Prosecution sought to introduce a revised version of a trial exhibit, the proper method would have been to have done so during Mr. Treanor's testimony or to have applied to re-open the case at the appropriate time. The accused submits that the Prosecution failed to do either. Appendix C in the eyes of the accused is an outrageous attempt to introduce unsworn evidence that was not subject to cross-examination. And furthermore, it constitutes a revision of unsworn testimony that -- sorry, I'm repeating. Which has not been subjected to cross-examination. There is a response in writing by the Prosecution dated or filed on the 16th of April. And I will just highlight the main points. First of all, the Prosecution submits that Appendix C represents a revised version of appendices 10.1 and 10.12 of Section 5 of the above-mentioned addendum did you mean. During Mr. Treanor's testimony on July 2nd 2003, the Prosecution advised the Court that it did not intend to call Mr. Aguirre, the author of that particular Section 5 of the report, but that he was available for cross-examination by the Defence. On 3rd July 2003, after that Mr. Aguirre had not been produced to give evidence in chief or in cross-examination, the Prosecution stated that those appendices would be rechecked and that the Trial Chamber and Defence would be provided with any discrepancies. The Defence did not object at the time. With respect to the same appendices, the Prosecution stated -- Appendix C, the Prosecution added, in Appendix C, exhibit numbers have been added to both the documents showing the implementation of the crisis staff decisions and conclusions, and the ARK Crisis Staff documents listed in appendices 10.1 to 10.12. The text of the documents listed has been shortened to focus only on implementation. The documents listed in those appendices which have not been admitted into evidence are not included in Appendix C. Documents listed in those appendices which do not directly indicate implementation are not included in Appendix C. Duplicate documents listed in the appendices have not been included in Appendix C. And the same appendix contains documents showing implementation of the ARK Crisis Staff decisions which were admitted into evidence after the report was tendered; for example, with regard to the Bosanski Novi and Prnjavor Municipalities, or documents which were not included in those appendices. Above all, the Prosecution contends that it is not attempting to introduce new evidence. Although Appendix C in its eye, it's obviously based on an original document, it should be treated as no more than a schedule of evidence tendered through the documents admitted into evidence. And the same, if the Trial Chamber is of the view that such a schedule would not assist it, then it may disregard it. The Trial Chamber has examined carefully Appendix C, and it has taken a long time, and that explains why we are coming with the decision today and not before. And it has examined carefully Appendix C within the parameters of the submissions made by the respective parties and particularly with a view to establishing that the submission of the accused that by means the Appendix C "the Prosecution is attempting to introduce new evidence before the Chamber in the form of a revised revision of a purported section of a previously admitted exhibit is founded or unfounded. Furthermore, this Trial Chamber perused this same Appendix C with a view to assessing or making an assessment on the assertion by the Defence that "this revision is unsworn testimony which has not been subjected to cross-examination." The conclusion that the Trial Chamber has come to is that Appendix C as explained by the Prosecution in their response indeed reflects or describes the exercise which the Prosecution made to update already existing documents on the basis and in the light of evidence which had been tendered until then, until after that the report had been prepared and after that Mr. Treanor had given evidence. The Trial Chamber has tried to find out if indeed there was any evidence that was being introduced obliquely and/or abusively by the Prosecution, and until now has found none. Neither has it come across any unsworn testimony or evidence which has not been subjected to cross-examination and which is being indirectly and nonetheless introduced abusively by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber, however, wishes to make it clear that it does and will continue to treat Appendix C, as suggested by the Prosecution itself, namely as no more than a schedule of evidence tendered through the documents admitted into evidence and not beyond that. This further motion of the accused is, therefore, also rejected. I thank you. We will reconvene tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask before -- I know we've run over. Would Your Honours also order that public versions of the motion filed by the Defence and by the Prosecution be made so that the public can see what Your Honour has been summarising. Your Honour, for one reason alone, and it may be because these wild allegations were being made Your Honour gave more detail to the Defence motion than to our response. And I am anxious that our response is seen in full. The confidentiality aspect was the reference to witnesses in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You will understand, Ms. Korner, that this was an oral decision. I mean, obviously we had prepared a few things in writing. But we did cover, I can assure you, we did cover all your objections just the same. But yes, provided the confidentiality aspects that regulated the matter so far is given due attention and redactions are made, I would recommend to the other two Judges to grant. However, I would like to hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think you have in your order touched upon the major allegations, the major contentions of our motion, so it is now -- that is now public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think anything is to be gained by going through that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you. One final point --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I don't think your answer -- if Mr. Ackerman now in public, because this has been given in public, this judgement, withdraws the allegations that he made against this Prosecution team and this office, that these matters were dealt with -- were put in improperly, Your Honours have now accepted there is no basis for that. But I would like a public withdrawal. If not, then I would like published -- I would like for the public to be able to read - I'm sorry - the sort of allegations that were being made and our responses because we gave a very full response pointing to the same kind of conduct in the Defence brief, but without making the same allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to state anything else, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not withdrawing anything, and I think you have covered what was in our motion very completely in the order you just entered for the record. I think that's all that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, point taken, Mr. Ackerman. But again, I mean, the oral decision obviously did not cover all the points. We covered what we considered to be essential for the purpose of the oral decision. I had more points here which I skipped, as I went through, reading the points, the notes that I had made. Yes, the decision is to grant that they be made public, but all due care has to be taken, I suppose. I don't know who is supposed to be charged with that, whether it's the -- the parties themselves. The parties themselves are to see to the proper redactions necessary needed to make the motions ready for -- to be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, since this is of interest to the Prosecution and not to us, I have no objection to the Prosecution making whatever redactions they think are appropriate from my motion and letting it be filed that way. But I really don't want to go through that exercise. I have plenty other things I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it's our application, yes, we'll do the appropriate redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you. I would like to make a public statement, one minute, which I would like to be communicated to the President of this Tribunal. I wish to thank all -- first of all, the parties for bearing with us, for staying here 20 minutes, the staff, the clerical staff here, and the rest of the team. I consider you on board. You're part of the team, all the technicians, all the interpreters, you have been most kind, you have been gracious. Without your cooperation, we wouldn't have managed to finish this part of the proceedings today. Once more, I thank you. You have behaved like this throughout the entire trial, and I wish to commend you. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same stuffy courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.05 p.m.,
